#2934. National League club 'loving limelight' ahead of FA Cup

A non-league football club is gearing up for one of the biggest days in its history as it prepares to host 2021 winners Leicester City in the first round of the FA Cup.

Oxford City will welcome the foxes to the MGroup Stadium at Court Place Farm in the hopes of adding to the list of great FA Cup upsets on Friday night.

The Hoops currently sit second in National League North, with their opponents 10th in League One - a whole 64 places higher in the English football pyramid.

Justin Merritt, Oxford City's chief executive, said the club was "loving our bit in the limelight".

He said the club's staff behind the scenes had been "working tirelessly" to prepare the ground, which is about a tenth the size of Leicester's, for the game.

"We've brought in extra stands and all sorts of things like pop up hospitality areas, bars - hosting three and a half thousand people is not the norm for us," Merritt said.

The Hoops have had a good start to their National League North campaign, having won eight and drawn three of their first 14 games.

Merritt said the players were "really up for" Friday night's cup tie, and that they and the club were ready to "give a fantastic account of themselves".

"Eight times out of 10 you'd expect a team three leagues above to win with a strong squad, but there's always those two times," he said.

"We'll be giving it every single thing we can, and we're really hoping to show what a great club we are and what a great set of players and we have."

Hoops midfielder Scott Pollock is a boyhood Leicester City fan [Getty Images]

Among those players is midfielder Scott Pollock, who scored the winning goal in the final qualifying round to send the Hoops into the first round proper.

Pollock is a boyhood Leicester City fan and said Friday's tie "just felt like it was meant to be".

"Obviously as a Leicester fan myself, I knew there was an option for us to get them in the next round," he said.

"I think at home we've got a good chance of going through."

The 25-year-old had unsuccessful trials at his boyhood club as a teenager, and instead found his way into the game through the Hashtag United YouTube team.

But he's now ready to get one back on the team that he still supports.

"A lot of my dad's side are from Leicester so they're all supporting them," he explained.

"It'll be quite funny when they're watching it on TV supporting me but then also supporting Leicester."

#2931. ‘There's no magic potion:' Vic Fangio pinpoints the issue with Jonathan Greenard

'There's no magic potion:' Vic Fangio pinpoints the issue with Jonathan Greenard originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Jonathan Greenard, the Eagles' $98 million free agent edge rusher, doesn't have much to show for his first two months as an Eagle.

Two tackles, one quarterback hit and one forced fumble (that the Eagles didn't recover) to show in 118 snaps over parts of five games.

"What I see is a guy that has had very, very little practice," Fangio said Tuesday. "I mean, when I say very little, minuscule.

"He missed all of training camp, missed the first two weeks of the season, no practice, started practicing, was on a pitch count, played 19 plays, was going to increase the next week, got hurt early in that game, didn't finish that game, didn't play the next game, and he's been limited in practice."

Greenard hasn't had a full week of practice yet. The Eagles, 2-6 with a six-game losing streak, open the practice week on Wednesday for a home game Sunday against the Giants.

Greenard has had exactly six days of full practice so far this year – the Friday before the Bears game, all three days leading up to the Rams, the Friday leading up to the Panthers and the Friday before the game Sunday night in Washington.

"You know, contrary to some people's popular belief, practice is important," Fangio said. "And he has had next to none."

Greenard missed all of training camp and the first two games with a pectoral injury, played 18 snaps against the Bears and 19 against the Rams, then missed the Jaguars game with an ankle injury. He's played 24, 29 and 28 snaps the last three weeks with modest results.

Prior to the Cowboys game, Greenard was limited on Thursday and missed practice Friday and Saturday. Last week, he was limited at practice on Wednesday and Thursday and full on Friday.

When he has played, Greenard hasn't been close to the player the Eagles envisioned. This is a guy who had 24 ½ sacks in 2023 and 2024 and made a Pro Bowl in 2024. His $24.5 million average annual salary is 12th-highest among all NFL edge rushers.

"Practice," Fangio said. "You know, there's no pill, there's no magic potion. You can watch all the tape you want, you can sit in meetings all you want, you can do walkthroughs all you want. The guy's got to practice. Practice is important for everybody."

The Eagles could sure use some pass pressure.

Nolan Smith has four sacks but he's the Eagles' only edge rusher with any sacks. Overall, the Eagles have just 10 sacks, 4th-fewest in the league and the fewest in franchise history through eight games.

You always take Pro Football Focus grades with a grain of salt, but out of 118 edge rushers who've played at least 100 snaps his 57.1 overall grade ranks 93rdand his 65.1 pressure grade ranks 77th.

According to Stathead analytics, Greenard has no quarterback hurries, and he's played the 6th-most snaps among all edge rushers who have no sacks or hurries.

"Yeah, he's just not into a groove," Fangio said. "He's not comfortable in our system totally and what we want him to do. And it's not because he doesn't know or doesn't want to. It's just he hasn't executed it. Walk-throughs are an assignment check. It's not execution.

"I don't know that I've had a guy that's had so little practice."

#2930. Robinhood shares fall as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses

Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.

Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.

Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.

Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

—With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney

#2928. 10 things you need to know about new Eagles quarterback Joe Milton

10 things you need to know about new Eagles quarterback Joe Milton originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Joe Milton on Sunday will become the Eagles' third starting quarterback this year and the first former Cowboy to start at quarterback for the Eagles in more than 30 years.

What fruit is Milton famous for throwing the length of a football field? What long-time Eagles safety went to the same high school as Milton? Who's the only other quarterback drafted by the Patriots to play for the Eagles?

You'll find answers to these questions and several other fascinating nuggets in our 10 Things you Need to Know about Joe Milton.

Guaranteed it's more interesting than 10 Things you Need to Know about Andy Dalton.

1. Milton's cousin is Anquan Bolden, the long-time Arizona Cardinals wide receiver, who caught 1,076 passes for 13,779 yards in his 14-year career. Both went to Pahokee, Fla., High School, also the alma mater of long-time Eagles safety Andre Waters. Another cousin of Milton's is Kevin Bouie, the Eagles' 7th-round pick out of Mississippi State. Bouie, who also attended Pahokee High School, never got into a regular-season game for the Eagles but played for the Chargers in 1996 and Cards in 1997.

2. Milton spent the first two years of his college career at Michigan, backing up Shea Patterson. During the 2020 COVID season, Milton started three games but gradually lost playing time to Cade McNamara and then transferred to Tennessee before the 2021 season. Milton was hurt most of 2021 and backed up Hendon Hooker for most of 2022, although he did win two late-season starts after Hooker suffered a torn ACL in a game against South Carolina. Milton went 8-4 in 2023 with 20 touchdown passes and five interceptions, passing for 2,769 yards and rushing for 292 with six more TDs.

3. Milton was originally the Patriots' 6th-round pick in 2024. He played in one game in New England, going 22-for-29 for 241 yards and a 48-yard touchdown pass to Kayshon Boutte in a 23-16 win over the Bills on the final day of the 2024 season after Drake Maye played one series. Milton also ran for a touchdown. Patriots head coach Jerod Mayo was fired soon after the game ended. Milton's passer rating of 111.4 was highest by a Patriots rookie since Bailey Zappe had a 118.4 in a game against the Browns in 2022

4. Although Milton has thrown about a quarter as many career passes as Tanner McKee – 202 to 53 – the strong-armed Milton has two more completions of at least 35 yards than McKee. Milton threw a 48-yard TD to Boutte in 2024 and a 35-yarder to Jalen Tolbert for the Cowboys in a 44-23 loss to the Broncos last October. McKee's longest career completion is the 34-yarder to Eli Stowers on the final play of the loss to the Commanders Sunday. In his career, Milton has averaged 8.0 yards per attempt and 11.5 yards per completion, compared to McKee's 6.1 yards per attempt and 9.8 yards per completion. Among 79 active quarterbacks who've thrown at least 50 passes, Milton's 8.0 yards per attempt is 3rd-highest behind Brock Purdy and Maye and his 11.5 yards per completion ranks 22nd.

5. Milton will become the Eagles' first quarterback to start a game after joining the team after opening day in 33 years. In 1993, the Eagles signed Ken O'Brien on Oct. 4, and he started four games, going 0-4, the last four starts of his career. O'Brien, who had made two Pro Bowls in nine seasons with the Jets, made his first start as an Eagle against the Cowboys on Oct. 31, 27 days after he signed. Milton will top that, starting against the Giants on Nov. 8, only 23 days after the Eagles acquired him on Oct. 16.

6. Milton will become the first quarterback from the University of Tennessee to throw a pass for the Eagles since Pat Ryan played in four games at the end of 1991. Ryan threw no touchdowns and four interceptions as an Eagle and had a passer rating of 10.3, worst by an Eagles quarterback who threw at least 25 passes since 1943. The Eagles' only other Tennessee quarterback was Johnny Butler, who threw 13 passes in 1943 and lost his only start, 13-7, to the Brooklyn Dodgers at Ebbets Field in 1943. Previous quarterbacks who've played for both the Eagles and Cowboys include Cunningham, Rodney Peete and Mark Sanchez. Only Peete played for the Eagles after the Cowboys.

7. Milton will be the second quarterback (and third player) drafted by the Patriots to throw a regular-season pass for the Eagles. Matt Cavanaugh, the Patriots' 2nd-round pick out of Pitt in 1978, spent 1986 through 1989 with the Eagles backing up Ron Jaworski and Randall Cunningham. He went 1-1 in two starts for the Eagles, both in 1986. Cavanaugh spent 13 years in the NFL – four with the Patriots, three with the 49ers, four with the Eagles and two with the Giants. He was 8-11 in 19 career starts with 28 touchdowns and 30 interceptions. After retiring from the NFL, Cavanaugh coached with the Cards under Buddy Ryan, the 49ers under George Seifert, the Bears under Dave Wannstedt, the Ravens under Brian Billick (where he was Cunningham's final NFL offensive coordinator), the Jets under Rex Ryan, the Bears again under Marc Trestman, Washington under Jay Gruden, the Jets again under Robert Saleh and he's currently a senior offensive with the Commanders under Dan Quinn. The only other player drafted by the Patriots to throw a pass for the Eagles was safety Joe Scarpati, the Patriots' 13th-round pick in 1964. He was 1-for-2 with a three-yard completion to Sam Baker in a 1968 win over the Lions at Tiger Stadium.

8. Following Jalen Hurts, Andy Dalton and McKee, Milton will become the fourth Eagles quarterback to throw a pass this year. Last time four quarterbacks threw a pass for the Eagles in the same season was 1991 when five did – Randall Cunningham, Jim McMahon, Brad Goebel, Jeff Kemp and Pat Ryan.

9. How strong is Milton's arm? You can find the video online, but while he was at Tennessee he threw an orange an estimated 100 yards. Milton, during a practice at the Vols' 80-yard practice facility, hurled the orange from his own end zone across the field and into the facility's back wall. He is said to have thrown a football 100 yards as well and a baseball 95 miles-per-hour.

10. Tradition in Pahokee is for kids to chase and catch rabbits that scatter when local farmers burn the sugarcane fields in the fall. According to local tradition, the faster you are and the more rabbits you catch, the better football career you'll have. Milton even has a tattoo of a rabbit on his arm to honor the tradition. Another Pahokee native, Janoris Jenkins, a Pro Bowl cornerback with the Giants, actually went by Jackrabbit Jenkins during his 11-year NFL career to commemorate his hometown tradition.

#2927. 76ers' Joel Embiid assessed postgame flagrant 1 foul by NBA for kick to Pistons' Cade Cunningham

Philadelphia 76ers center Joel Embiid was assessed a postgame flagrant foul 1 for kicking Cade Cunningham in the first quarter of Wednesday's 112-106 win over the Detroit Pistons, the league announced on Thursday.

The play in question occurred at the 5:32 mark of the first quarter. With Cunningham defending him at the 3-point line, Embiid kicked out with his right leg on an initial shot attempt before passing to LeBron James. His kick struck Cunningham in the groin, causing the Pistons guard to bend over in pain.

Cunningham was slow to recover as Embiid cut past him for a dunk. He also trailed behind as play went to the other side of the court, grabbing the area that was struck. No foul was called on the play.

Whether it was the pain from the kick or perhaps frustration from no call being made, Cunningham only had nine points in the first half before finishing with 26 (shooting 1-for-9 on 3s) and 11 assists.

During Wednesday's game, Embiid was whistled for a technical foul for shoving Detroit's Tolu Smith under the basket with 1:25 remaining in the first half.

By NBA rules, a player assessed a flagrant foul 1 — defined as "unnecessary contact committed by a player against an opponent" — during the regular season receives one point for the infraction. Accumulating six points results in a one-game suspension. Wednesday's flagrant 1 penalty was the first for Embiid this season.

Two flagrant 1 fouls during a game results in ejection. A flagrant 2 comes with an automatic ejection.

Embiid tallied 26 points and 15 rebounds in the Sixers' win, which improved Philadelphia to 8-1 (4-0 on the road). Jaylen Brown led the 76ers with 30 points, adding 7 rebounds.

#2925. If you stayed up late enough, you saw why the Eagles are so high on Eli Stowers

If you stayed up late enough, you saw why the Eagles are so high on Eli Stowers originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Eli Stowers said two weeks ago that whenever he did finally get the opportunity to make plays, he was confident he'd be ready.

Then he went out Sunday night and showed he was.

It was largely garbage time and the game was all but over, but Stowers – the Eagles' rookie 2nd-round pick – caught three passes for 53 yards in the second half of the Eagles' sixth straight loss. They were the first three receptions of his career in the second game of his career.

Stowers caught a seven-yarder from Tanner McKee for a first down in the third quarter and then caught passes on the final two snaps of the game, a 12-yarder that gave the Eagles a 4th-and-7 on the Washington 42-yard-line with two seconds left and then a 34-yarder down to the 8-yard-line as time expired.

"It's always good to get the first one out of the way and to be able to feel that in a game," Stowers said at his locker after practice Wednesday. "Anytime you go out there and you get a first catch, that's a blessing to be able to even say that, 'I got my first catch in the NFL game,' so I think it did help the confidence.

"My body's been feeling better and been able to move a little better so it felt good."

After a middling training camp, Stowers spent the first six weeks of the season on Injured Reserve, and it was fair to wonder what exactly the Eagles had in this converted quarterback from Vanderbilt. He made his NFL debut in the loss to the Cowboys and had one target but no catches.

But anyone who watched till the end of the game Sunday night got to see the soft hands, athleticism and speed the Eagles like enough about Stowers to make him the 54th player and second tight end taken in this year's draft.

He actually almost scored on that final snap of the game before finally getting tackled at the 8-yard-line after the longest pass play of McKee's career.

"I caught the ball and it was a lot of space," he said. "And so anytime you catch the ball, you've got to go try to score. That's the mindset that any ball carrier should have. So that was my mindset. I was hoping I could drag them in there. They ended up getting me down, but it's all right."

What's really important is that Stowers is healthy after a lost summer. The Eagles didn't rush him back, and it paid off.

"I had hurt my hamstring and then I hurt my quad and then it was a span of like seven weeks where I just had to get my body back healthy from camp," he said. "I don't think it was really a matter of me being behind physically. It was just I had to get back healthy, get on the field and perform well."

Stowers became the Eagles' first 2nd-round pick to not play the first six weeks of a season since guard Bobbie Williams in 2001. Williams wound up playing 12 years in the NFL and starting 136 games, mainly for the Bengals.

"Sometimes injuries like that, you can't do anything about it," he said. "Take care of your body the best way you can. Get good sleep, eat right, drink, do all the stuff. But sometimes you just can't do anything about it. So if you sit there and you stay on it, kind of sulk about it, nothing's going to get any better. So I just attacked it every single day of getting it back right and be prepared for when I get back."

It's no coincidence that the Eagles put Stowers' locker next to Zach Ertz, whose 828 career catches are 5th-most in NFL history by a tight end.

The Mexican manager also discussed his relationship with Mourinho, recalled a memorable victory against Real Madrid and explained why improving Valencia's position matters more than the occasion itself.

#2921. $6.3 billion Binance hack is largest crypto theft on record

Binance said Friday that a security incident impacted about $6.3 billion in client assets, with around $3 billion frozen on-chain, marking the largest crypto hack on record.

The company later added it began recovering assets impacted by the breach after pledging to cover losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users, which the company created in 2018 as a protection for clients in the event of a hack.

It wasn't clear how the attack took place. The world's largest crypto exchange initially said the hack may involve "a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions." However, Co-CEO Richard Teng later said the attack involved a more complex process rather than the misuse of a single engineer's permissions.

The FBI said Friday it was aware of the incident and was in touch with "relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate ​potential impacts, ​and ⁠coordinate appropriate investigative steps."

It wasn't clear either who was responsible for the breach. But TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence and AI investigations company, pointed to North Korean hackers as the potential culprits. "Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack and the KelpDAO hack in April 2026: small Tornado Cash withdrawals funding an operator wallet, staging that began well before the theft, and signatures obtained in advance then executed in one burst," the company said in a post.

Blockchain data platform Chainalysis also said this appears "be the work of North Korean cybercrime group TraderTraitor. This group has repeatedly targeted the cryptocurrency industry, exchanges, DeFi protocols, and investors, to raise funds for the regime. We base our intelligence assessment on on-chain activity observed in the hours following the hack."

Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals while it overhauls its withdrawal security systems and has revoked the affected address authorizations, Teng said. The exchange is also working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms to trace and recover the stolen funds, while deposits remain unaffected.

Binance co-founder Yi He said deposits remained unaffected and continued to operate normally, while the exchange was working on enhancements to its withdrawal service and related address controls. It expects to begin resuming withdrawal services within the next 48 hours.

"We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak. We will share a detailed technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete and the facts are fully verified," Binance said.

The announcement followed moves by several crypto firms, including Circle Internet Group, Tether and Ripple, to freeze funds tied to the hack.

Exploits are not uncommon in the crypto space. In 2025, Bybit suffered roughly $1.5 billion in losses due to a hack. More recently, Bitget lost more than $350 million worth of digital assets in a cyber theft incident. Over the past several years, bad actors have also drained billions of dollars in crypto from decentralized exchanges.

This week's breach "proves our exact point in proposing regulations for crypto markets earlier this month," Michael Selig, chairman of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, said Friday in a CNBC "Squawk on the Street" interview. The U.S. derivatives regulator on Oct. 5 proposed a framework that would effectively put crypto exchanges under federal government oversight — after Congress failed to approve legislation to regulate the asset.

"The real issue here is that these are unregulated offshore exchanges, and they don't have the same sorts of safeguards that we have in our financial markets here in the United States. We want to offer a federal option to these exchanges to come and register with the CFTC, and they would be subject to the same sorts of cyber security safeguards that we have in our markets today," he said.

Bitcoin fell more than 4% to $77,187.60 on Friday as the hack weighed on crypto markets.

Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire said Thursday evening in a social media post that the company had frozen more than 800 million in USD Coin associated with the incident. USDT stablecoin issuer Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino also said in on X that his firm had frozen more than 1.5 billion of its stablecoin that may have been related to a potential breach.

Jack McDonald, Ripple's senior vice president of stablecoins, said it was actively freezing affected funds held in RLUSD, its U.S. dollar-backed stablecoin.

#2919. I’m an athletic trainer – here’s how to know when kids sports are too intense

At a recent T-ball game, I was talking with another father who mentioned that his son had never played before. As we watched our children falling over trying to scoop up a ground ball, we laughed about how they were still figuring everything out. There was something refreshing about seeing kids learn a game without worrying about how well they were playing.

That moment stayed with me. I've spent years as an athletic trainer in collegiate and professional sports, helping athletes stay healthy, handle the demands of competition and perform at their best. Today, I'm a clinical associate professor of kinesiology and chief health and performance adviser for an NCAA Division I athletics program. Given my work, you might expect me to take an active role in developing my own children's athletic abilities, especially in a youth sports culture where early specialization and greater commitment are often seen as advantages.

And I understand the appeal. Like any parent, I want my children to have opportunities, and it's easy to wonder whether another practice or lesson might help them get ahead. But with twins who are nearly 6, I'm more interested in whether they enjoy sports than how good they become at them.

As they get older, particularly if they want to pursue sports seriously, my role as a parent will change. Right now, I can step back and let them explore. But as training and competition become more demanding, I'll want to become more involved in understanding and questioning those demands. Research on training, recovery and athletic development can help parents navigate what's appropriate as their children's sports experiences intensify.

Experts recommend that children engage in a wide variety of physical activities before specializing in one sport.

When I'm watching my children play, I'd rather be their dad than their performance coach. When they ask to practice hitting or throwing, I'm happy to help. They usually decide when we're done. Twenty minutes? Great. Five minutes? That's fine too.

Practice matters, but giving children some control over when and how they practice can help keep it from becoming another obligation.

Research involving more than 9,000 young athletes found that children tend to be more motivated to participate in sports when parents support their ability to make decisions about their participation.

As children get older, their goals may change. Some will want to compete at higher levels or focus on a particular sport. Those ambitions deserve support, but giving children a voice doesn't mean parents should step away from important decisions. As commitments grow, parents may need to ask more questions about training schedules, recovery time and the expectations placed on their children.

I've heard parents describe traveling hours for youth sports tournaments, only to discover that many of the teams competing came from the same communities they had traveled from. One parent recalled driving to Houston for a tournament where six of the eight teams were from the Dallas-Fort Worth area.

I understand how families end up in these situations. An extra practice, private lessons or joining a more competitive team can each seem reasonable. Over time, those commitments become expectations, and saying no isn't always easy when your child is part of a team.

But more training doesn't automatically produce better athletes. My experience in sports medicine and performance has taught me that improvement depends on how athletes respond to training, not simply how much they do. Training places demands on the body, and athletes need time to adapt.

The American Academy of Pediatrics cautions that excessive training and early specialization are associated with increased overuse injury risk and may contribute to burnout. Risk depends on training volume, recovery and individual development, particularly during adolescence.

Persistent soreness, unusual fatigue or declining enthusiasm can be a sign of burnout for kids in youth sports. Klaus Vedfelt/DigitalVision via Getty Images

As training demands increase, parents should pay attention to how their children are responding, not just whether they're experiencing pain. Persistent fatigue, declining performance, changes in sleep or a loss of enthusiasm may suggest that recovery isn't keeping pace with training. Even an athlete who loves their sport can reach a point where the demands become too much. These are reasons for a parent to discuss the workload with their child and coaches, while persistent or worsening pain warrants medical evaluation.

Athletic development also benefits from variety. Running, climbing, jumping and exploring different activities can help develop coordination and a range of movement skills. The International Olympic Committee recommends varied physical activity and developmentally appropriate training, including for children who may eventually specialize.

Just as important is whether young athletes want to keep playing. Children who enjoy sports are more likely to want to continue participating, research shows. When young soccer players were asked what made sports fun, they identified working hard, improving and spending time with teammates. Even the best training program won't accomplish much if an athlete no longer wants to participate.

In collegiate and professional sports, reviewing performance is routine. After competition, staff identify what worked, what didn't and what needs attention. But children don't need a performance review every time they climb into the car.

I let my children start conversations about their games. If they want to talk about a missed ball, something funny or something that upset them, I'll listen. If they want to talk about something else, that's fine too.

Researchers who recorded parent-child car rides around sporting events found that much of the time passed in silence and sports came up relatively infrequently. They also observed occasions when parents interrupted or provided feedback before children could respond. The findings don't establish one right way to handle the drive home, but they offer parents a reason to consider whether their children want feedback in the first place.

No parent knows whether their child will become a competitive athlete, play recreationally or eventually find interests outside organized sports. I'm comfortable leaving that future open for my children. As a father, I'm far more interested in whether my kids will want to play again next week than how well they played today.

This article is republished from The Conversation, a nonprofit, independent news organization bringing you facts and trustworthy analysis to help you make sense of our complex world. It was written by: Adam Annaccone, University of Texas at Arlington

#2917. Jaguars' point differential of +108 this season is 50 points better than any other team

No NFL team is dominating opponents like the Jacksonville Jaguars.

After blowing out the Ravens 33-10 on Thursday night, the Jaguars have now outscored their opponents by a cumulative score of 229-121 this season. That's a point differential of +108, by far the best in the NFL.

The team with the second-best point differential in the NFL is the 49ers, at +58. The Jaguars' point differential is 50 points better than the next-best team.

At 6-2, the Jaguars do not have the best record in the league, as the Bills, 49ers and Vikings are all 6-1. The 49ers are favored to beat the Raiders and improve to 7-1, and the Bills and Vikings play each other on Monday night, so the winner will be 7-1.

But at the midway point of the season, point differential is a better indication of a team's quality, and a better predictor of a team's future success, than win-loss record. That's because with as small a sample size as half a season, a few plays in a few close games can skew the won-loss record, but a few plays don't skew point differential. Historically, the teams that prove to be the best over the course of a season are the teams that win some blowouts, even if they also lose some close games.

Winning blowouts and losing close games is exactly what the Jaguars do. Both of the Jaguars' losses were one-possession games that were tied in the fourth quarter, while the Jaguars' wins have included some massive blowouts: The Jaguars' 35-point win over the Colts was the biggest blowout of this NFL season, their 29-point win over the Patriots was the fourth-biggest blowout in the NFL this season, their 24-point win over the Browns was the seventh-biggest blowout in the NFL this season, and Thursday night's 23-point win over the Ravens was the 11th-biggest blowout in the NFL this season.

The Jaguars have won four games by more than 21 points this season; no other team has more than one win by more than 21 points.

Jacksonville has a 3.5-game lead in the AFC South, and six of the Jaguars' nine remaining games are against opponents with a losing record. They're poised to run away with their division, perhaps earn the No. 1 seed in the AFC, and maybe blow some teams out in the playoffs just like they have in the regular season.

The Titans would have no motivation to move Dike with him only in his second season, but with Jeffrey Simmons already gone, it would cause no harm for the 49ers to at least call. If San Francisco does pull the trigger, Dike would become one of the best returners in 49ers history on day one if he continues his pace he's shown in Tennessee.

Dike has 94 kickoff returns so far in his season and a half with the Titans. Only five players in 49ers history (Super Bowl era) have taken more than 75 kickoff returns (Vic Washington, Ted Ginn, Maurice Hicks, Carl Monroe, and Dexter Carter), and Dike's 25.7 yards per those 94 returns would rank second behind only Washington.

The same would apply for punt returns as well. Dike has 34 of those to his name, and while plenty of 49ers (Super Bowl era) have taken at least 30 punt returns (23 to be exact), none are better than Dike's 15.7 yards per punt return."

#2914. The midterm election could reshape the muni bond market. Here’s what investors need to know

The outcome of Tuesday's election is expected to have broad implications across the market, including municipal bonds.

The spotlight has been on the battle for congressional control and whether Democrats will wrest the House of Representatives, the Senate or both from Republicans. But for the muni market, what happens at the state level could have bigger repercussions — at least in the near term.

There is an array of initiatives on ballots around the nation that could change tax laws and add to bond supply. Taxes matter to muni investors since the income received is free of federal tax, as well as state tax if the holder lives in the state where the bond is issued.

Depending on the location, ballot measures are up for approval that would either provide tax breaks, or raise taxes on the wealthy.

"It's a complete bifurcation between red and blue states," said Dan Close, head of municipals at Nuveen. "Blue states are trying to put in place graduated income tax structures, trying to capture more revenue from high-income earners. Red states are promoting affordability by trying to cut property taxes."

Red states are those that predominantly vote Republican, while blue states swing toward Democrats.

For instance, California has a proposition known as the "billionaire tax," which would impose a one-time levy equal to 5% of the wealth of certain taxpayers with at least $1 billion in assets. The state also has a measure on the ballot that would make a temporary tax hike permanent on individuals earning over $371,000, adjusted annually for inflation. The tax is currently set to expire in 2031.

"The impact to the muni bond market will be to make the exemption more valuable," Close said of the possible passage of tax increases. Investors will likely seek shelter in the muni market, which would send bond prices higher, he noted.

It is a different story in Florida, where voters are set to decide whether to increase the Sunshine State's homestead exemption for non-school district property taxes. Qualified homeowners currently have a $25,000 property tax exemption, as well as another for $25,000 that doesn't apply to school property taxes. The new proposal raises the latter exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 by 2028. New residents have a five-year waiting period before receiving the benefit.

If passed, some local governments will have to find other revenue sources or increase the overall tax rate to replace what they've lost, said Tom Kozlik, head of public policy and municipal strategy at HilltopSecurities.

"It's not necessarily going to result in downgrades for sure, but there would have to be some balancing with regard to overall revenues," he said.

Not all municipalities will be hurt equally, which means credit research is important, said Close.

"Like everything in municipal finance, it is really on a case-by-case basis that you could have some credit deterioration from [a] rollback of property taxes," he said.

Other voters on Tuesday will be asked to approve more state or local government debt. That could weigh on a market that has already seen heightened supply.

Some $473.8 billion has already been issued year to date, through September, according to the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association. That's a 7.8% increase over the same period a year ago. In 2025, total muni issuance reached $587.3 billion, 14.3% higher than 2024, Sifma said.

Cooper Howard, director of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research, believes supply is the biggest issue coming out of the election.

"That amount of issuance has been one of the reasons why you have to see that strong amount of demand continue to keep pace with it for total returns to keep up," Howard said.

Fortunately, new supply doesn't necessarily come quickly into the market. "There's a window over a couple years that they can issue," he noted.

The ultimate makeup of the next Congress could also have consequences for muni investors as lawmakers sort out their priorities. Most notable is what lawmakers will do to tackle the country's affordability problem, Kozlik at Hilltop said.

"There could be some tax policy initiatives and even affordability-related initiatives that manifest themselves in the first quarter of next year," he said. "That could impact housing. It could impact higher education. It could impact public power financing."

Investors considering moves before the election may want to look at those states with tax increases on the ballot, said Close at Nuveen.

For instance, Nuveen recently began offering a separately managed account dedicated to Washington after getting an enormous number of inquiries from financial advisors. The state recently enacted a 9.9% tax on individuals with taxable annual income above $1 million, set to go into effect in 2028. But the issue is now being put to voters, who can decide whether to repeal the new law.

"At the margin, if you do think that some of these measures are going to pass, knowing that bonds usually move up with an increase in taxes, there might be some opportunities to buy ahead of the election for blue states," Close said.

Howard believes munis are attractive right now, particularly for those who are in a tax bracket of 24% or above. Fundamentals are good and the bonds largely have good credit quality, he said. "About 70% of the broad muni index is either triple-A or double-A rated."

Kozlik is also bullish, calling yields "really attractive." He suggests investors concentrate on AA-rated or higher bonds.

"The muni space is part of the portfolio that most investors want," he said. "It helps them sleep well at night."

#2913. What we learned from the Spurs win over the Mavericks

At some point between the end of the '21 season and the start of the '22 season, I made a pact with myself: no more first quarters.

You have to understand, these were dark times to be a Spurs writer.

And yes, I know, as a fan myself, that those years were no more of picnic for the average fan than they were for me, but still. There's just something about watching a beating and then having to write about it that feels vaguely abusive, especially when some of your favorite people are still involved.

Having to watch Gregg Popovich lose like that…I felt like a journalist covering Muhammad Ali's last fights.

It didn't matter how valiant he was, how much he tried to make something out of nothing — it just seemed kind of dirty to watch at all. We all knew what he was doing, of course.

But watching a worthy sacrifice doesn't make it any easier. I still get misty-eyed when the Iron Giant tells Hogarth Hughes not to follow him (as if he could) before rocketing from the ground into space, and meeting the falling arc of a nuclear warhead.

There's a reason I don't watch the movie all the time. It would be fairly masochistic of me to do so.

But there are 82 games in a season, and someone has to cover them.

As a writing staff, you take some solace in the knowledge that you're all in this together. You're all having to write about it. You're all having to dig for silver linings. And that (for this site) you're all doing it out of some (possibly misplaced) sense of love for the team, and the sport, and the readers who are just about as miserable as you are.

But I just could not watch first quarters anymore. Not in real time.

It's one thing to know that the Titanic is sinking; to be thrown into the middle of the chaos and do your best to make sense of it. It's another thing altogether to watch the ship headed towards the ice-burg in the darkness. To hear the godawful scraping and know what it means. To have been watching the journey for years, and completely run out of ways to spin it.

It had to have been a very conscious decision on James Cameron's part to make that movie a romance. How else could you get people to watch it? The wreck just cannot be the main course.

I couldn't convince myself to watch the game at all if I started with the first quarter. The Spurs would either start taking their beating from the onset, or worse, soar to an early lead that we all knew wouldn't last.

So I decided that I would start watching during the second quarter, finish the game, and then watch the beginning.

It was so much easier to bear when you already knew how it would end. Especially when the Spurs did miraculously pull off the win.

You could go back and break down how the positive momentum started, with the empty but understandable hope that there might be something algorithmic in those 12 minutes that could be reverse-engineered and employed more regularly.

And even the sting of defeat didn't smart as much when you were able to initially avoid the fool's gold of productive opening minutes.

Hell, sometimes it was even a little funny when you encountered the Spurs finding a way to lose the opening frame that you'd never even considered.

(Even though the Spurs won the game, I don't think I'll ever forget Jakob Poeltl picking up 2 fouls in the first 96 seconds of the Lakers game in 2022 that tied Pop with Don Nelson.)

Lately, though, I've been forced to reconsider my first-quarter policy, and the reason is pretty obvious: Victor Wembanyama is just too fun to be put on the back-burner in any capacity.

It was a sensible policy when the losses were piling up. Sometimes it still is.

But frustration with a contender-caliber team starting slowly is simply not enough to deprive myself of the immediacy of the joy provided by the most insane fusion of Hakeem Olajuwon, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, and Wilt Chamberlain imaginable.

Wemby just had the first *official* 50 point, 20 rebound, 8 block game in NBA history (and the first 50/20/10 in the non-assist category if you combine his steals and blocks), in his 8th game of his 4th season, and he's the same age that Wilt was as a rookie!

Chamberlain didn't even peak until he was 25!

That's the territory we're in. That's the conversation.

And that's in spite of existing in the era of injury and rest management. In spite of the fact that Wemby's doing it on a team that's good enough to have already made the Finals.

In spite of playing in an era where blocks are harder to come by, and strategic scouting and game-plans are another level, and players are (pretty successfully) bombing away from long range. In spite of an out-of-whack jumper that's converting at about 28% outside of 10 feet.

Having chugged a 16oz energy drink during my late dinner before the game in an attempt to battle the somnolent rigidities of middle-age, I found myself doing the same 'fighting the urge to pee' dance that my child still breaks out every now and then, as I tried to hold out til the end of the half.

Smelling weakness through the television screen like a shark loose in a blood bank, Wemby proceeded to block three shots in roughly 13 seconds, as if to say: are you sure that you want to miss this?

I can't remember the last time I almost wet myself over basketball, or a more satisfying pee at the half.

There's plenty of negative things I could say about the game. I don't know that I've ever seen this team shoot that badly as a whole. Even Julian Champagnie and Devin Vassell couldn't buy a shot.

There's no reason it should have been that close with such a performance out of Wembanyama.

The bench's defense looked like it had been coordinated by Wile E. Coyote and the Acme Corporation, and they put up a total of ten points in their relief of the starters. Carter Bryant and Tarris Reed somehow got no minutes on a night in which it couldn't have been more clear that a shakeup was needed.

Even De'Aaron Fox's previously next-level show of efficiency took the wrong turn at Albuquerque.

This was a bad game, if we're being honest. A real stinker. And yet I can't find the animosity within me to make this the all-around feel-bad roast that it should be, because, as I've said so many times over the last year, it just did not matter.

This should have been one of those games where I had to go back and break down the first quarter in a state of rage.

It should have been. But I just don't have it in me to despair the undespairing.

Through it all, Wemby was completely unshaken. Understandably, so were his teammates. In their shoes, I think I'd feel the same way.

I don't love that they frittered away lead after lead. I don't like it as a trend, and I don't like it as reminder.

But I think it's easy to forget that we don't live in that place were I can't stand to watch the first quarter anymore, and that by resigning myself to that policy of the past, I'd be getting in the way of my own happiness.

You can't protect yourself from pain without also protecting yourself from rapture. I think sometimes, in both life and basketball, we have a way of forgetting that.

I can tell you everything they did wrong. I can rant and rage with the best of them, and sound my barbaric yawp over the roofs of the world.

I can tell you that they were saved anyway, undeservingly.

Give me a better story than that, I dare you.

I don't have a lot of nice things to say about this game, but man has Wemby really taken to the responsibility of attacking the rim this season. Right now he and Giannis are the only players in the NBA averaging 7+ Rim FGs and 8+ Paint FGs made per game. And Wemby's actually doing it more ways than Giannis is, as the only player in the league averaging 5+ points as the P&R Roll Man, 4+ Points off of Cuts, and 4+ points In Transition, per game. If his jumper starts heating up, we're going to see even crazier numbers than we did last night. Which is insane when you consider that he's 4th in the league in scoring with a jumper finds the bottom of the bucket about 1/4th of time right now.

It's been a bit of an uncomfortable fit for Stephon Castle when all three guards are on the court at the same time, and he seems to have been asked to serve as more of an off-ball shooter because of that, but when the need arises, he always seems to find an extra gear. I know many are hoping that the addition of Tobias Harris forces some rotation adjustments, but I will say, Castle is getting the open shots, and he's not shrinking from the challenge. He's shooting 32% from three now, but if he starts hitting those, that lineup might really morph into something scary, because everything will open up on the inside, and Wemby's already mutilating the rim as it is (and Harper's been slouch, either). And as much as I think Harris will be a boon to the team, I'd secretly prefer to see that happen instead.

Though Fox had probably his most inefficient night of the season on the offensive end, he's still the only player in the NBA creating 15+ Assist Points Per Game, with a 2-1 Assist-to-Turnover Ratio, while also sporting a 65+ True Shooting Percentage, which is crazy when you see all the names that miss the mark. But, just as importantly, he's been outstanding on the defensive end, and it showed in the clutch last night when he kept the still-lethal (and long-time Spurs killer) Kyrie Irving off-balance just enough to that his attempt at a game-winning bucket. To have lost a game with Victor playing like that would have felt catastrophic, so he'd be next in line for the game ball, in my mind.

Third-year guard Bronny James and rookie guard Cameron Carr have been assigned to G League Coachella Valley, the Lakers announced Thursday.

#2909. Drake Maye’s early-season turnaround earns him October honors

New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye was named AFC Offensive Player of the Month for October.

The award comes after Maye led the Patriots to a 3-1 record, completing 67.2% of his passes for 1,199 yards, 12 touchdowns and just two interceptions. He also added 129 yards and two touchdowns on the ground.

Maye became the first Patriot to earn the honor since Tom Brady during the 2017 season.

"That's something to be proud of for Drake," Patriots offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels said. "I always look at those things as team achievements. Certainly nobody's going to win an individual award in football without all the guys that do their jobs around him. I think you celebrate that as a group.

"He's certainly deserving of it, and a lot of credit to him for just kind of improving as September finished and got into the next month of the season. A lot of little things he did better, and hopefully we can continue to do that."

It marked a significant turnaround for Maye after the 24-year-old struggled to open the season. The quarterback was perhaps the biggest reason the Patriots found themselves with a 1-2 record through the first three weeks, throwing just one touchdown against six interceptions.

Improved ball security has been one of the biggest factors in Maye's resurgence. He has thrown just one interception over the last four weeks, while his 1.2% turnover-worthy play rate in October ranked third among qualified quarterbacks.

Additionally, Maye's trademark deep ball has returned despite the Patriots losing several of their top pass catchers to injuries, while has has operated as one of the league's better quarterbacks when dealing with pressure.

"He has worked really diligently for two years now on becoming a better passer from the pocket," McDaniels said. "Everybody talks about how his athleticism is, and it's great, and he made another great play outside the pocket last week. But I'd say he'd probably be more excited about the one that he slid to the right and climbed up into the pocket, and makes the throw down the field to Kyle [Williams]. So I think he's worked really hard at it.

"I think it's repetition and I think it's confidence in the protections. I think that's where it stems from."

Maye's November started strong as well as he scored three total touchdowns to lead a come from behind win in Miami. The quarterback will look to keep things going against the Green Bay Packers this Sunday.

#2904. Washington Commanders vs LA Rams Week 9: Five Questions with Turf Show Times

It's week 9 of the NFL season and the 2-4-1 Washington Commanders will be facing a 4-4 Rams team at home at Northwest Stadium on Sunday at 1:00 p.m. ET. The Rams started the season hyped as the best team in the NFL and presented as likely Super Bowl winners, but have struggled with consistency since then. At the same time, the Rams are a talented and well-coached team, having blown out the Giants 28-6 in Week 2 and the Chargers 24-9 last week.

On offense, the Rams are coached by head coach Sean McVay, offensive coordinator Nate Scheelhaase, and assistant HC Kliff Kingsbury, with McVay calling the plays. Two of those three coaches should be familiar to Washington fans as they were former playcallers here. This offense is built around one of the NFL's best offensive lines, a gap-scheme run game that favors power, and the NFL's highest use of 3-TE sets. It's an offense that sets up to bludgeon opposing defenses in the run game, but also uses their heavy personnel tendency to force opposing defenses to go heavy and set up star WR Puka Nacua to feast on heavier, slower defensive matchups. This kind of offense funnels the ball to Nacua, who currently leads the NFL with a 37.9% target share. A ruptured hamstring by WR Davante Adams will only increase the likelihood of the Rams going heavy and throwing the ball to Nacua. Overall, the Rams have the 3rd-ranked passing offense and the 6th-ranked rushing offense in terms of yards per game.

On defense, the Rams have been led by DC Chris Shula, who has worked his way up from being the assistant linebackers coach of the Rams in 2017. Shula has typically employed a 3-4 front with heavy use of zone coverage on the backend, though he is also known for extensive use of disguise, both on his pressure packages (faking a blitz from one direction while actually bringing pressure from another), and in his coverage (rotating coverages post-snap to confuse QBs). This year, after the Rams traded a 1st-round pick for shutdown CB Trent McDuffie, they have occasionally been using him to shadow star WRs, which allowed him to erase Malik Nabers in their Week 2 matchup. However, McDuffie's status is uncertain this week after sustaining a back injury against the Chargers. The Rams also just lost star CB Jaylen Watson to a season-ending shoulder injury, which could leave the backend of the Rams defense weakened. At the same time, Los Angeles may be getting back star pass rusher Myles Garrett this week, which would be a tremendous boon for their defense. Overall, the Rams have run one of the NFL's best defenses this year by many metrics, though it has ranked better against the pass (7th) than run (15th).

I asked Kenneth Arthur of Turf Show Times five questions to better understand the state of the Rams and what to look for in this game.

1) The Rams entered the season widely considered an elite team and Super Bowl favorite, but sit at 4-4 and on the outside looking in to win their division. Why has their season started off much slower than expected?

I'd start with revisiting why the Rams were considered such heavy favorites. A perennial contender under Sean McVay, the reigning MVP, then they add Myles Garrett, Trent McDuffie, and Aaron Donald, right? Garrett hasn't played since Week 1. McDuffie has missed a couple of games. Donald isn't more than a rotational option at this point in his career.

But that doesn't explain everything, right? Well, the Rams are the perfect example of an "Achilles" or a "Goliath". They look dangerous but they always have the same weak points. I wasn't convinced the Rams were Super Bowl favorites going into the season because they didn't fix special teams, they didn't use the draft to make their team better now, and they have too many players who are on the precipice of another injury, such as Puka Nacua, Davante Adams, and Matthew Stafford. Nacua has been banged up, Adams is out 6-10 weeks, and Stafford is dealing with elbow soreness. Jaylen Watson, another big free agent addition, has also been banged up and aggravated a shoulder injury on Sunday.

Special teams is awful, the receiver corps is thin, and the defense has predictable holes at linebacker. The defensive line was further weakened with injuries to Kobie Turner and Poona Ford.

Overall, it's a banged up team with bad special teams and they were very close to wins over the Broncos and Bills anyway. I think the bigger concern is losing to the Cardinals. However, Garrett is returning to practice this week, so it's possible we see the closest thing to the version of the Rams people thought they'd be when those predictions were made.

2) The Rams have had a disastrous performance on special teams so far this year. What are some of the specific problems the Rams special teams have faced, how are they dealing with them, and what do you think they will be like going forward?

The Rams have had bad special teams almost since McVay took over. He fired popular coordinator John Fassell a few years into the job and it's been downhill since then. L.A. won't focus any effort on finding a reliable kicker. They had Matt Gay and then let him walk in free agency over money. Now they're on their third kicker–but last week they had TWO active kickers, so they're almost on their fourth. Not locking down a good kicker is a big reason that the magnifying glass is on L.A.'s special teams.

Kickoff coverage has always been weak and the Rams don't even really try to understand the new rules. They are 27th in kickoff yard average and 32nd in punts that land inside the 20. Punter Ethan Evans has a big leg but won't be known for technique or accuracy, nor does he have good coverage. Special teams coordinator Bubba Ventrone (fired by the Broncos last season) is just the latest in a long line of people to have that job. He probably won't last long either.

The Rams have signed a few special teamers during the year in an effort to improve, like Grant Stuard and Alex Bachman, but it's not much and not having an impact.

They will continue to be bad moving forward. That's what I predict.

3) The Rams have been really efficient in the draft, with late-round gems like Puka Nacua, but at the same time have seemed to devalue high draft picks and preferred to trade them away for known NFL quantities. What do you think of this approach of GM Les Snead in recent years with respect to draft picks and roster construction?

I would disagree that the Rams have been "efficient", or even successful, in the draft. I think Puka Nacua is doing all the heavy lifting in that argument, but I'll give two more: Kyren Williams in the 5th and Quentin Lake in the 6th in 2022.

L.A. drafted three starting quality players on day two in 2023 (Byron Young, Steve Avila, Turner), and then RT Warren McClendon and Nacua on day three, and a couple of role players. That's all fine.

The biggest issues start in 2024, which is why the Rams are so thin at certain positions now. First-round pick Jared Verse was very overrated and that's proving out in Cleveland. Second-round pick Braden Fiske (the Rams traded a future second-round pick to move up for Fiske, one of the biggest day two overpays in history) has regressed. Third-round picks Blake Corum and Kam Kinchens are "OK". Then the Rams made six day three picks and none of them are consequential players, if they're even still on the team.

The 2025 draft saw the Rams pick six players, with second-round pick TE Terrance Ferguson on IR and yet to contribute much. Third-round OLB Josaiah Stewart contributes here and there, but we'll see how much higher his ceiling is. Four day three picks aren't contributing and two of them are off the team. Then the Rams drafted five players in 2026 and none of them contribute. One didn't make the team and two are healthy scratches.

So these last two draft classes include 11 players and the only ones even really playing are Stewart and seventh-round receiver Konata Mumpfield, merely out of necessity because of injuries.

These are picks that we may look back on in 2027 and say "Good job, I didn't respect your vision Les Snead."

This would imply that first-round QB Ty Simpson is playing next year and looks like a worthy pick at 13, which was much higher than most experts believed he should go. This would mean that L.A.'s two second-round tight ends in the last two years (Ferguson, Max Klare) are playing like an exciting 13 personnel duo. This would mean that they don't keep parting ways with the guys they draft within 1-3 years, as they've been doing a lot of recently.

The trades (2 firsts for Stafford, 1 for McDuffie, 1+Verse for Garrett) make sense to me really. I think late first-round picks are overrated. But it's times like this being 4-4 and struggling in certain areas that definitely call into question the Rams' draft and trade philosophies because they haven't been to the Super Bowl since 2021 and have only come close once. The Rams need to see a better return on investment, and fast.

One more note: I've been one of the biggest Puka Nacua fans in the world since he debuted in 2023. The fact that he's not certainly part of L.A.'s future at this point is concerning, to say the least, both because of what Puka has done to make the team doubt him and because the Rams don't seem to realize that they'll be one of the worst teams in the NFL without him.

4) Who is one Rams player on offense and one on defense that Commanders fans probably don't know much about, but should?

Nothing on offense is going to surprise you. Stafford, Nacua, and Kyren Williams are still the big three. The only other player who pops is Corum and I just assume everybody knows about him by now because of fantasy football. Corum is a more dynamic runner than Williams, but McVay hasn't lost any trust in Kyren. There might be a few extra passes to Tutu Atwell this week.

Quentin Lake is someone who doesn't get enough credit as an actual star. He plays deep safety, linebacker, and slot, in addition to lining up nearly anywhere else. He has three picks and 11 passes defensed. Good against the run and the pass. Lake deserves as much credit for his value as Nick Emmanwori in Seattle.

5) How should Washington gameplan for this matchup on both sides of the ball?

Defensively, if you contain Williams and Corum on early downs with heavy fronts and get the Rams to third-and-medium+, you really limit Stafford's options because the offense is so one-dimensional without Davante Adams. Keep a linebacker or safety down in the box on those plays to try and take away Puka's underneath routes because despite Puka being a very talented downfield threat, most of his production actually comes on short passes. Force Stafford to use his secondary passing weapons like Tyler Higbee, Colby Parkinson, and Mumpfield because they're inconsistent and unreliable.

Offensively, use quick throw passing plays to get the ball out of Jayden Daniels' hands quickly and avoid third-and-long plays where the Rams pressure has a chance to get home. No free points, so protecting the ball is probably more important than scoring touchdowns–if you give the Rams enough time, they will end up making a mistake or two on special teams and turn the ball over once or twice. Those are Washington's best opportunities to capitlize.

A companion article to this with my answers to Kenneth's questions will be linked here when it is available.

Thanks again to Kenneth Arthur for taking time out of his day to answer our questions about the Rams.

#2903. Game Preview #10: Wolves at Pelicans Game Thread

Fresh off of a tough win against a talented Houston Rockets squad, the Minnesota Timberwolves take on Zion Williamson and the New Orleans Pelicans on Friday night.

Who: Minnesota Timberwolves (6-3) vs New Orleans Pelicans (4-4)

Where: Smoothie King Center — New Orleans, LA

After starting the year 0-4, the Pelicans have ripped off four straight wins to claw back to .500. Sprinkled into that winning streak are some impressive victories over the surging Memphis Grizzlies (handing them their only loss on the season thus far) and the Atlanta Hawks. New Orleans is not a squad that is projected to climb the Western Conference standings or necessarily strike fear in the hearts of opponents, though they are still a team with enough competitive and ascending players to keep opponents honest.

Considering the still shorthanded state of the Wolves, they may have their hands full with a healthy-for-now Pelicans team. The win over the Rockets was thoroughly impressive, though Chris Finch and company will need to remain focused if they are to come out of this game with a victory.

Here are a few things I am looking out for against New Orleans:

You know the guys – the dudes who love to turn up and have career games against the Wolves no matter what state their team is in. Most teams in the NBA have at least one Wolf Killer. The Pelicans have a few.

Perhaps most obvious of these players is Zion Williamson, who averages a whopping 28.5 points per game against Minnesota, nearly five points higher than his career average of 23.8. When healthy, Williamson is one of the premier tickets in the league and can score at will against nearly anyone. Jonathan Kuminga and Rudy Gobert will have their hands full with Zion, who will seek to outmuscle and overpower anyone that Finch decides to throw at him.

Saddiq Bey is another player that ramps up his production against the Timberwolves. A career 14.8 ppg scorer, his number increases to 19.5 for his career against Minnesota. As a member of the Pelicans, Bey's average jumps up to 24 ppg versus the Wolves. The guy just flat out doesn't like us.

As the Pelicans have other surging young players contributing to their recent run of success, this matchup may be more difficult than initially expected. Derik Queen has looked to be a solid NBA big man and Jeremiah Fears has been becoming a more well-rounded player. If Minnesota's defenders can keep the Wolf Killers from transforming into much better versions of themselves, the game is there for the taking.

Bones Hyland is a fun player. He's energetic, has a great smile, and keeps the fanbase engaged with his aesthetically pleasing style of play and affable three-point shot celebration. He's an ideal bench player that could fit in on many teams. We are fortunate to have him as a Timberwolf.

However, with a slew of injuries that continue to hamper Minnesota's preferred personnel, Bones continues to be thrust into heavier minutes than he would normally get. In the four games before Anthony Edwards got injured, Hyland played an average of eight minutes per night. Since then, his minutes have doubled, playing 16 minutes per game in the five matchups since Edwards (and now Terrence Shannon Jr.) went down.

Bones's 19 point, eight assist night against the Los Angeles Clippers last week was a true representation of what he can bring as a player when he's on. It's unrealistic to expect that kind of production and efficiency from him most nights, though he does help the Timberwolves find tempo and form whenever things are going south.

If the Timberwolves are going to have any sustained success while Edwards and TSJ are out, Hyland will need to continue to exert efficiency and production in his limited time on the court. He was electric against the Rockets, scoring 19 points in just 16 minutes of play. For a team that continues to lose players at a high clip, Bones will remain an integral part of the offensive flow moving forward.

There's not much more that can be said about just how putrid Minnesota's free throw shooting has been. Currently the team sits at 63.4%, good for dead last and a massive 7% behind the next closest team, which is the 1-7 Milwaukee Bucks. Minnesota shot a cool 53% (10-19) at the line just last night versus Houston in a 10-point victory to bring that percentage down even lower. So it goes.

It's not like this team has a problem shooting the ball, either. That's what makes this ineptitude so baffling. The Timberwolves shot 53% from the floor and 43% from distance against the Rockets. And yet, while standing at the free throw line, uncontested and still, they can't put the ball in the hoop.

Two players on the Wolves are shooting greater than 80% from the line this season. Everyone else is below them. That is unacceptable.

It would appear that Gobert's inability to consistently make shots from the charity stripe (42.6% on nearly six attempts per game) is becoming contagious to the rest of the team. While it hasn't been the biggest issue the Timberwolves have faced this season, it will become one as the team enters more late-game clutch time situations. We're not far off from a few tight losses spurring a dialogue that laments the team's lack of efficiency from the line. The recent defeat at the hands of the Golden State Warriors comes to mind, poor officiating be damned.

Chris Finch will need to address this problem somehow. Unfortunately, getting reps from the free throw line will not show itself as immediately game-changing. It will take time. Finishing this season anywhere but dead last should be seen as a success at this point. Until then, Minnesota needs to figure out how to capitalize on the opportunities they are given.

#2902. Santoli: AI bull market almost surely needs tech stocks to recover to keep advancing

The road to bull-market glory does not run through Walmart and Berkshire Hathaway and Eli Lilly.

There's been a virtual buying panic in traditionally defensive, high-quality stocks over the past few weeks, a near-equal-and-opposite offset to the selling pressure in semiconductors and AI-build-out spenders. The three stocks above — the only members of the $1 trillion market-cap club not in Big Tech – have collectively added $550 billion in market value in the past month, almost making up for what Alphabet has lost.

The Nasdaq-100 and the S&P 500 Low Volatility ETF (SPLV) are rushing toward one another in a satisfying picture of symmetry that nonetheless reflects an almost comical level of tactical rotation executed by an investment community accustomed to playing one factor against another.

While this to-and-fro has so far protected the S&P 500 as a whole from an appreciable setback for months, it has left it stymied around levels that date back to May — before we got two earnings-reporting seasons showing 30% annual profit growth.

A week ago here, I suggested the AI theme was nearing a make-or-break moment to stage a recovery or risk surrendering its leadership status and destabilizing the broader market. Thus far, this trade has failed to respond to moderate oversold conditions or a run of cosmetically strong hyperscaler quarterly results, further loosening its grip on the benefit of the doubt.

In stressed markets undergoing soul-searching about the long-term bullish thesis, prices often need to travel further to find buyers with conviction while the market action must disappoint dip-buyers to extinguish complacency. Hard to know if we're there, but presumably we're now closer.

The Nasdaq-100 closed Monday right at its 200-day moving average, off almost 11% from its record high. After an enervating failed Monday-morning bounce attempt, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index finished down another 3.8% and settled under the late-July low that was set as the Situational Awareness hedge fund was finished liquidating.

"Markets did not get the memo that bearish seasonal pressure typically subsides in mid-October and instead ended the month with some of the most acute selling pressure that has been realized during the late-summer/early-fall period," notes JPMorgan technical strategist Jason Hunter. He's advising clients to remain on the defensive "until we see clear evidence of a bottoming process on the charts or until there are clear signs of capitulation."

This is a time-tested playbook, though many a sharp market pullback has ended without what would qualify as unqualified capitulation.

The market action is winning some plaudits for the way non-tech stocks have held up better, many groups benefiting from the "quality" rotation while abandoned consumer cyclicals get a reprieve from easing oil prices and the slide in the 10-year Treasury yield back below 5%.

This gives active managers plenty to do in playing against a highly concentrated and tech-dependent S&P 500. But I'll continue to argue that the bull market built on the AI story will almost surely need the AI story to get back on track to keep advancing. A prolonged period when the equal-weight S&P 500 outperforms the market-cap-weighted version is otherwise known – usually – as a bear market.

The AI-related stocks' weighting in the S&P 500 is off the highs but remains near 45%, according to Morgan Stanley.

As the chart shows, AI has wobbled relative to the rest of the market during this uptrend before reasserting itself.  But there's a trickier element to the current gut check: In prior phases of the buildout, the key limiting bottleneck gave investors something to buy in order to exploit it.

The initial scarcity of GPUs meant to own Nvidia above all else from 2023 through 2024. When cloud capacity, power and cooling were found to be the crucial scarce resources, hyperscaler stocks worked and the AI-adjacent industrials were drastically revalued. Then memory emerged as the chokepoint and Micron and Sandisk went stratospheric.

Now, as Nvidia's Jensen Huang has said, capital is the constraint and that not only leaves no asset to buy, but it raises the cost of capital broadly as the mega-caps go free-cash-flow-negative.

Overlapping feedback loops and scrambled correlations across the markets and the real economy have further sapped investor conviction. Treasury yields no longer move with oil but largely with AI-capex sentiment, with both in retreat lately. AI-stock setbacks also mute inflation momentum and the equity wealth effect, meaning fewer Federal Reserve rate hikes are anticipated now versus a month ago.

This all probably sounds like an elaborate trap, and it has become one for the previously crowded trades. Could this reflect the end game for the AI-exuberance market chapter, which as I keep pointing out peaked around the SpaceX IPO in June? Impossible to say for sure, but if it were, I'm not sure things would look much different to this point.

But I don't want to dismiss the possibility that a lot of the known challenges are largely reflected in prices.

I argued in August that we should assume the valuation peak for this cycle was in. We've now retrenched to a forward P/E of 18.5 on the S&P 500 from 23 a year ago and the Nasdaq-100 at 20x is at the slimmest premium to the S&P 500 valuation in nine years. I'm on board with the idea that the market is telling us companies are now "over-earning," but if nothing else there is less valuation risk now than in recent months.

Sentiment toward AI stocks is in the dumps. Funds' positioning in tech has retreated below neutral. Important trading lows this year have happened near the turn of the month on March 30 and July 29, and the Nasdaq-100's relative-strength reading is exactly as oversold as it was at those turns.

So, stay alert for possible relief bounces that could evolve into something more consequential if indeed the midterm elections pass in a way that allows traders to unclench a bit into the year's home stretch.

John Kolovos of Macro Risk Advisors on the latest reading: "Similar to valuation, sentiment is not a timing tool, but it is getting harder and harder to find any bulls, as a near-perfect storm of tight financial conditions is being met with tech earnings that have gone from bad to worse in the blink of an eye."

-Another good big-picture conversation on the practical business and investment implications of the next phase of AI proliferation on Patrick O'Shaughnessy's Invest Like the Best podcast, this one with investor Cliff Sosin. His comparison of AI infrastructure economics to internet connectivity providers and his argument for how most of the productivity boost will go toward "consumer surplus" rather than corporate profits are particularly interesting.

-For my birthday Monday, my colleague and friend Sara Eisen wondered how I would write a birthday message to myself. I immediately regretted suggesting she ask ChatGPT, which generated this credible and somewhat embarrassing result:

"Another year older, though the longer-term trend remains constructive. Some modest deterioration in the underlying internals, perhaps, but nothing that suggests a decisive breakdown.

"The candles on the cake are approaching historically elevated levels, though valuation concerns have persisted for years without derailing the advance. At this stage, the key question isn't whether I've gotten older — that's largely priced in — but whether the wisdom gains can continue to offset the inevitable compression in energy multiples.

"For now, I'm maintaining a cautiously optimistic outlook, with upside optionality, downside support from family and friends, and no immediate need for Fed intervention. Happy birthday to me. The secular bull market remains intact."

The stampede into perceived defensive stocks has been a crucial driver of Apple shares' massive outperformance over the Nasdaq-100 since the AI-capex agita flared up months ago. Apple heading into Monday's earnings report had outperformed the Nasdaq-100 by nearly 20 percentage points over the prior six months.

Its singular refusal to join the aggressive spending binge to build AI capacity preserved its free cash flow and made it the perfect counterweight to the capex trade, while inflating Apple's valuation to a 15-year high.

But its advantage in free-cash-flow yield has now narrowed, thanks to its stock-price gains and the collapse of peer shares.
