#2901. Bengals News: Salute to Landon Robinson

It's November, which means two things when the Cincinnati Bengals are concerned.

One: Joe Burrow and the offense have woken up from their annual offseason slumber (that extended a little too far into the season, as usual).

With Veterans Day just a few days away, the NFL is in its military-appreciation month, and the Bengals happen to have a defensive tackle from the Navy and a Marine on the roster. After being named the Bengals' Salute to Service Award nominee, Landon Robinson spoke with Bengals.com's Geoff Hobson about his time at Navy, his service, and his future before the team left for Spain.

The Bengals selected Robinson with the No. 226 pick in the 2026 NFL Draft. That's the same pick the Arizona Cardinals spent on former NFL safety and former Army Ranger Pat Tillman.

"I took a class where we did a case study on him [Tillman] and learned about his story and what he did in the NFL and made the decision to go serve. When I saw I got drafted 226, 'Wow, that is crazy,'" he said when he was asked about the coincidence by Hobson.

DJ Turner, key Bengals get injury updates from Madrid

Quite a week for Turner, the No. 1 cornerback who appeared to suffer a serious injury just one week ago. The fact the Bengals even had him board the plane overseas, though, was a big hint he had a real chance to play.

'That's the Only Glaring Need That They Have' — Ex-Bengals WR Pushes Cincinnati To Make Trade for 3-Time Pro Bowler

"I like the Bengals," Hawkins said about the best fit for Taylor. "I think that's the only glaring need that they have offensively. Joe Burrow obviously can throw for 450 yards a game, but is that sustainable? Especially as you get later in the season and into the playoffs. They have a great schedule ahead of them. #2900. 4 things to watch as the Mavericks’ Cup quest continues against the Utah Jazz

The Dallas Mavericks (4-4) will meet the Utah Jazz (1-7) 7:00pm CST Friday at American Airlines Center in the the group stage of the in-season NBA Cup tournament. Dallas enters this contest on a two-game slide after their comeback attempt Wednesday against San Antonio came up short, 112-111. After a challenging stretch of the schedule to begin the season, the Mavericks face their second opponent this week to bring a record with fewer than two wins into the AAC; Monday the Sacramento Kings improved to 1-6 against a Mavericks team without Kyrie Irving, 115-100. The Jazz arrive having dropped six straight after the Pelicans prevailed Wednesday in overtime, 120-113. The Mavericks and Jazz share a common opponent this week, as Jazz fell Monday to the Spurs, 119-97.

The Jazz organization's goals remain more focused on developing their young core than immediate playoff contention, but in dealing for forward Jaren Jackson Jr. last spring, CEO Danny Ainge moved beyond the rebuilding phase of angling for draft position with a trade that greatly bolstered the team's chances (and expectations) of winning now. Jackson's departure against the Grizzlies Oct. 26 with a torn MCL means that the team will turn to the stockpile of talent amassed in recent drafts, like forward Ace Bailey, guard Darryn Peterson, and point guard Keyonte George.

All three of those players seem to have bright futures, but it is Lewisville's George who has emerged as the most NBA-ready player as of this writing. The big guard hit some big shots against New Orleans Wednesday, icing a jumper that seemed to have won it before replays revealed that the ball left his hands a split second late, then knocking down the first six points of overtime coming off high screens from center Lauri Markkanen. Though the Jazz got blown out by the Spurs Monday, the previous matchup of these teams Oct. 28, a 117-111 OT Spurs win, provided some insight as to how this Jazz team can be dangerous. Playing in their first game since the Jackson injury, George keyed a Utah comeback with a drive and layup that tied it in the final minute, and guard Brice Sensabaugh made the three that set up George's heroics, plus another three in overtime.

For the second time in a week the Mavericks face an electric scoring guard from the 2026 draft class. Sacramento's Darius Acuff's 10 of 21 performance against Dallas Monday improved his season shooting percentage to .406. Utah's Peterson, shooting 34% on the season, has shown flashes of his handle and shot creating ability, but at times has looked like a rookie trying to find his role in the offense.

Markkanen, the Jazz' other veteran big man who appears ready to win now, has been tested in Jackson's absence, chasing a 2-11 three-point shooting performance against Portland with an excellent 4-7 effort from deep against the Spurs. After disappearing for much of the second half against the Pelicans, Markkanen emerged in the final two minutes of regulation to drill a three that brought the Jazz to within one and a pair of foul shots that pushed them in front a possession later. Shouldering the load as Utah's primary frontcourt threat (starting center Jusuf Nurkic is out with a toe injury) has exposed Markkanen's strengths and flaws alike. Wednesday the Jazz produced their second 40-point quarter of the season in the third, as Markkanen and reserve center Mohamed Bamba pushed and stretched a small Pelicans lineup around the floor and the Jazz attacked the rim relentlessly. But when New Orleans went big late, Zion Williamson, Derik Queen, and Saddiq Bey all got the shots they needed against Markkanen.

Some of the Mavericks' most effective stretches against the Spurs came with PJ Washington Jr., Morez Johnson Jr., and Caleb Martin taking turns as the biggest Mavs on the floor, as Dallas' small lineup cut into the Spurs' lead even after Victor Webanyama re-entered the game. If coach Dusty May employs a similar strategy against Utah, Markkanen and Bamba will have to cover a lot of ground to keep up.

Friday's game will be the Mavericks' second of the group stage of the in-season tournament and the Jazz' first. Dallas beat Houston Friday, 116-111, to notch a 1-0 record in the group stage and a +5 point differential. Dallas trails Denver for first place in West group A, as the Nuggets' +7 point differential after their 127-120 win against Phoenix Friday gave them the tiebreaker.

Mavericks guard Walter Clayton Jr. appeared in 45 games for the Jazz last season with averages of 6.8 points and 5.5 assists before being included in the Feb. 3 trade with Memphis that brought Jaren Jackson Jr. to Utah. Jazz guard Josh Green, a Maverick fan favorite from 2020-24, comes off the bench for 3.0 points per game, and is still making things happen with hard cuts and hustle plays.

Friday's game will be shown on MAVSTV+ and KFAA Channel 29. Radio broadcast is 105.3fm KRLD (English) and 99.1fm KFZO (español).

#2899. Giants news: Cam Skattebo still sidelined, Malik Nabers wins monthly honor, more

Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know as the Giants get ready to face the Eagles in Philadelphia this Sunday.

This is inherited franchise history for John Harbaugh and the 2026 New York Giants, not earned.

But it's notable history nonetheless, resurfacing every time the Giants' buses hit the Turnpike and travel to what has become a house of horrors for this organization. The head coaches have changed. The players have changed. So have the circumstances.

The Eagles were supposed to win the NFC again. If they were going to fight for the title in the division, it was supposed to be with the Cowboys. Now those teams have a combined record of 5-11 and the Giants are talking about being buyers at the trade deadline instead of sellers, maybe even with Jonathan Taylor, one of the star running backs of the league, for a long time.

For now, it starts with McCarthy, clearly sold and mightily by one Harbaugh to another. Twenty-three years old. Giving Giants fans the kind of hope that J. Dart did last season. With a chance to be as great an in-season acquisition as the Giants have ever had if he keeps going like this, and if they keep going. Door wide open for the Michigan kid, and his coach, and his new team. They just have to make sure the Eagles don't slam it in their faces on Sunday.

John Harbaugh reaffirmed his confidence in kicker Dominic Zvada on Wednesday, saying the New York Giants are looking for consistent results but are not concerned about the position. The coach noted that the staff continues to evaluate technique and fundamentals, with the clear expectation that kicks will travel straight through the uprights.

"We're looking for kicks to go between the sticks, right through the upright, straight. Looking for straight kicks," Harbaugh told reporters. "But you're also looking at the technique and the fundamentals, but we're not worried about him."

Luxury target: Taylor might cost too much for a New York squad that's already down its fourth- and fifth-round picks in the 2027 draft, but what about Derrick Henry? If the Ravens decide their season is up without Lamar Jackson on the field, Henry could be a potential trade candidate. He's owed only $650,000 over the rest of 2026 and $12 million in 2027. And while the future Hall of Famer has struggled for most of the season, playing with a more mobile quarterback in McCarthy might help create some running lanes.

Bargain target: With the Chargers still winless, Harbaugh could call up former Ravens executive Joe Hortiz (and brother Jim Harbaugh) and attempt to make a move for Dalvin Tomlinson. The well-traveled defensive tackle has slipped as a pass rusher from his 2020-24 peak, but Tomlinson would be a rotational player for a Giants team that's barely getting by on the interior.

New York Giants: Defensive Interior. Given how they have played early in the season and the Philadelphia Eagles' struggles, the Giants have a serious chance of winning the NFC East. Since it is John Harbaugh's first year in New York, they probably shouldn't mortgage the future to get better this season, but they could add someone next to DJ Reader on the defensive line. Reader has earned a 90.4 PFF grade to lead all interior defensive linemen so far this season, but he is their only player at the position to have played at least 50 snaps and earned a PFF grade above 55.0.

External NFL sources, not from within the Giants building, vary in whether they believe a Taylor trade actually gets done. Several sources SNY touched base with are hellbent in their conviction that Harbaugh will do whatever he can to get him, seeing an opportunity for New York to make a run. Others, familiar with what the Colts are asking for, believe the price is so steep Indianapolis isn't actually interested in dealing him. He'll remain with them throughout this season, with a trade revisited in March.

Still, their stance to this point is the right one. Do everything you can to help your team accomplish that … within reason. They shouldn't waver. Harbaugh must fight the temptation to do more over the coming week.

#2898. Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac rally as Ackman presses for conservatorship exit

The midterm elections could be a turning point for the release of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac from government control, according to billionaire investor Bill Ackman.

Investors may agree with him, if the rally in both stocks is any sign.

The Federal National Mortgage Association, known as Fannie Mae, and Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation, or Freddie Mac, have each jumped more than 60% from Oct. 14 to Monday's close. The stocks were both up roughly 3% on Tuesday.

Ackman, the founder of Pershing Square Capital Management, has long pushed for the two entities to be released from federal conservatorship.

"The reason why it's not being touched right now is, you know, midterms," he said in an interview with CNBC's "Squawk Box."

Ackman, who owns both names through Pershing Square, believes Freddie and Fannie have the potential to increase "10-fold from current share prices," he said in his quarterly letter to shareholders, issued on Monday.

Fannie and Freddie buy mortgages from banks and other lenders, and then package them into mortgage-backed securities, known as MBS. Their operations are critical to the housing market, providing liquidity to banks and creating a secondary market for MBS.

The entities were placed into conservatorship in September 2008, during the financial crisis. The stocks were delisted from the New York Stock Exchange in 2010 and have traded over the counter since then.

Ackman wants the conservatorship to end, arguing the entities would be worth multiples of their current valuation if they were freed from government control.

President Donald Trump has supported ending the conservatorship of Fannie and Freddie. But it remains politically and economically contentious.

The entities operate under strict capital threshold requirements and would need to be recapitalized, which could happen through issuing common equity. However, the Treasury Department would need to figure out an exit plan for its roughly $388 billion ownership stake in the entities through preferred securities and warrants.

Congress may also need to play a role, passing legislation to restructure the government's role in mortgage financing and home-loan guarantees.

Nonetheless, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently said it could happen before Trump's term ends, telling 2Way's "The Morning Meeting" podcast that the administration will tackle the ownership structure "next year, the year after." He said affordability will be guiding the decision.

One point of controversy is whether ending the conservatorship of Fannie and Freddie would increase the spreads on MBS over Treasuries, effectively making mortgages costlier. Bessent has sought to reassure the market that wouldn't happen.

"Whatever we do is going to be guided by making sure that the spread on [agency] mortgages … over the Treasury does not increase," Bessent said.

Ackman argues that privatizing the GSEs would help insulate them from political meddling. "Fannie and Freddie are these massive, enormously profitable institutions where whichever political party controls them…if they're still in conservatorship, can influence the outcome of elections," he told CNBC.

In one scenario, he explained, Democrats win the White House, conservatorship is still in place, and Democrats push Fannie and Freddie to lower credit standards in order to expand home ownership and affordability.

"If they're going to move more aggressively into borrowers with lower credit quality, for example, to achieve a political objective, that's going to have an impact on trillions of dollars outstanding mortgage securities," Ackman said. "It's going to have an impact on overall credit spreads."

MBS investors want certainty about how the entities will be run, he noted.

"That only gets resolved in a world in which they exit conservatorship, they become publicly traded companies that are owned by institutional and retail investors," Ackman said. "We set the rules. In conservatorship, the president can do anything."

Carmelo Anthony and La La Anthony (née Vázquez) reportedly have reached a settlement agreement after almost a decade-long split.

Although terms of the separation are confidential, there was a pending judgment of divorce that needed approval from the New York County Supreme Court as of Wednesday, according to People.

Once the former MTV VJ and the NBA star receive the official imprint from a judge, they'll be newly minted singles.

La La filed for divorce from the NBA star back in 2021, citing irreconcilable differences, according to TMZ, which first reported on the settlement Wednesday.

The couple began dating in 2003 after being introduced through a mutual friend, DJ Clue. They became engaged on Christmas Day 2004 and three years later welcomed their son, Kiyan Anthony, now a 19-year-old sophomore at Syracuse University, where he is playing college basketball.

The two tied the knot in July 2010 in a New York ceremony with hundreds of guests, among them sports and entertainment stars including LeBron James, Spike Lee, Serena Williams, Ciara, Kim Kardashian and Ludacris, The Times reported.

Reports of their separation surfaced in April 2017, and by August of that year, Carmelo had welcomed a daughter with ex Mia Burks.

Although the Anthonys reconciled in late 2018, they ultimately called it quits in July 2019, according to People.

La La was already using a divorce label despite it not yet being official.

In a 2022 episode of Alex Cooper's "Call Her Daddy" podcast, La La opened up about her split from Carmelo, saying that there were still difficult moments, especially regarding the co-parenting of Kiyan.

"I learned how strong I am," she said when asked about what she'd learned from the divorce. "You just find yourself getting stronger and stronger. What do they say? Like you don't know how strong you are until being strong is your only option."

La La also shared that the demise of their marriage began around the time that Carmelo was traded from the Denver Nuggets to the New York Knicks in 2011.

At the time of the 2022 interview, she shared that her perspective on love had changed. "I just don't know if it's in the cards for me," she said on the podcast.

However, in a more recent October interview on "The Jennifer Hudson Show," she revealed she was "open" to dating and that this was her "season of being open" for someone who is confident and adventurous.

As for the NBA Hall of Famer, he was rumored to be dating Racquel Smith, the widow of former NFL defensive end Will Smith. The two were seen together in June.

#2896. Binance breach puts custody at center of crypto infrastructure trade

The $6.3 billion Binance hack could accelerate a shift in how investors value cryptocurrency companies, putting a greater premium on custody providers and the infrastructure needed to securely hold and protect digital assets.

Much of crypto's evolution this year has involved companies moving past their reliance on trading volumes and transaction fees, to focus instead on building the infrastructure connecting digital assets with traditional finance. Last Thursday's breach adds a new dimension, bringing cybersecurity, custody, compliance and balance-sheet resilience into sharper focus.

Importantly, the Binance breach was not an indictment of crypto itself, or a case of leadership-driven fraud, as with FTX in late 2022. Instead, Binance's leadership moved quickly to contain the fallout, protect customers and commit the exchange's own resources to cover losses.

On Tuesday, Binance CEO Richard Teng told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" that the company has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets, and that it is still in the process of purchasing outstanding, more illiquid assets.

Management's response, alongside efforts elsewhere in the industry to boost confidence, helped prevent a security breach from escalating into a broader crisis of confidence. For example, Tether, Circle, Ripple and others moved quickly to freeze or restrict access to about $3 billion in stolen assets; Coinbase blocked transfers to compromised wallets and offered Binance direct assistance.

The hack could even help shape the next phase of the crypto infrastructure trade. The new winners may not just be the businesses with the most users, volume or assets under custody, but the ones that can also demonstrate they're able to protect those assets under extreme duress.

"Which company has the resources to invest in cybersecurity and protect customer funds? For a smaller company, it could be much harder because once these crypto companies become infrastructure plays, providing the well for tokenization … they need to have the compliance and control in place so that a similar hacking will not happen or can be minimized," Owen Lau, senior analyst at ClearStreet, told CNBC. "Larger companies have more resources that could give them some advantage."

While institutional investors have increasingly embraced digital assets, broader adoption depends on confidence that those assets can be securely held, accessed and transferred. The Binance breach highlights the importance of that infrastructure, and could increase demand for specialized custodians and platforms with established asset-protection capabilities.

Coinbase has operated a dedicated institutional custody business since 2018. Circle entered the custody business this year, after the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency granted it approval to operate as a trust bank. In the past few years, Ripple and Kraken have also launched custody businesses.

Still, smaller players compete in the space as well. Small cap crypto exchange stock Gemini Space Station has offered custody services since 2019. BitGo Holdings, founded in 2013, is one of the earliest players in institutional crypto custody and infrastructure, with a reputation for security and serving major institutions.

The shift could also drive consolidation as companies look to buy capabilities, deepen their infrastructure offerings and achieve the scale needed to compete, Lau said.

The more consequential structural shift may be the separation of custody from execution, according to Morgan Stanley.

"Crypto exchanges have historically combined trading, custody, and settlement within vertically integrated platforms, concentrating operational risk. Repeated security breaches could encourage investors to move assets toward independent custody while continuing to trade on CEXs," the firm's analyst Felix Stratmann said in a note Monday," referring to centralized cryptocurrency exchanges.

"This would preserve the role of centralized exchanges as liquidity and execution venues, while potentially benefiting regulated custodians, including banks, as institutional investors place greater emphasis on asset segregation, operational resilience, and investor protection," Stratmann said.

#2895. Jonah Coleman continues to turn heads with the Broncos

The rookie running back consistently takes advantage of the opportunities he gets on the field and runs with them, literally. In the 28-24 win over the Kansas City Chiefs, he had the game-changing reception that set up his game-winning touchdown.

Now comes the next chance for Coleman on Sunday against the Carolina Panthers and their 30th-ranked rushing defense.

When Broncos head coach Sean Payton was asked how Coleman has impressed despite the injury, Payton said:

"We had those glimpses in the spring and in training camp and in the preseason. Atlanta, there's a run, it just stood out to you. So the one thing that was unique about him is oftentimes you don't get to see them in third-down protection plans, but he was someone that we had quite a bit of tape on. Advanced protection plans, and he's built to handle the blitz.

"It's one thing to know who I have, but then also to be strong enough to do it. I would say that there were three backs — we just saw one of them that we really had visions for. Each one may be a little differently, but his versatility, to your point, that doesn't always — you don't get to stamp that with a lot of rookie backs that you feel like they're going to develop into. We saw enough that we felt like he was going to be a good third-down protecting back as well, with the way he was built."

In the victory over Kansas City, Coleman finished with 11 carries for 41 yards and a touchdown, as well as four receptions for 63 yards. Obviously, that total is boosted by the 51-yard reception to put Denver on the 4-yard line.

But it's clear the rookie brings an element to this offense that the other running backs on the roster cannot. Coleman has shown great vision, instincts, and runs with physicality that is fun to watch.

"I think he's playing really well with confidence," Broncos quarterback Bo Nix said to the media. "He's a very intelligent young running back. What sticks out the most is he can handle a lot. You can put a lot on his plate. After we learned that R.J. Harvey wasn't going to play last week, he got a little bit more of the bulk of R.J.'s stuff.

"It's impressive to see him be able to be used in a lot of different ways. When he gets in there, he's a natural runner. That's what he's drafted for. That's the position he plays. It's the out-of-the-backfield stuff that I think is making a good impression on us right now."

What's most impressive is how Coleman is handling pass protection. That's one of the toughest aspects for a rookie running back to grasp. What's exciting to contemplate is that Coleman can get even better the more he plays.

"We caught him in the right pressure there," Payto said to the media. "Yes, he's very comfortable. He's a different type (of) player than RJ (Harvey), but there were a lot of traits to like. More importantly, there was the exposure in an offense that sometimes the player just doesn't have that exposure, so you can't know for sure. I think we knew a little bit more with his tape."

All of this to say, Coleman brings a spark to the Broncos.

"I think that started since rookie minicamp, and then the preseason game against Atlanta, and then the Jacksonville game, and now this game," Broncos offensive coordinator Davis Webb said to the media. "I think every time he gets an opportunity, he's showed up. His teammates love him. He's smart, he's mature, and he's going to continue to get better, which is awesome."

#2886. Democratic sweep puts crypto on defensive in Washington

Democrats' sweep of Congress likely resets the political calculus for crypto, ushering in a more adversarial approach in Washington and pushing industry-friendly legislation like the Clarity Act to the back burner.

With crypto critics like Sherrod Brown, D-Ohio, returning to the Senate and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., retaining significant influence over financial policy, analysts say the new Congress is likely to focus on scrutinizing President Donald Trump's personal crypto dealings over supportive industry legislation.

For years, crypto fought an uphill battle in Washington, asking for clear operating rules, but often landing on the receiving end of regulation by enforcement. That shifted after Trump's 2024 election victory, giving the industry a reprieve and seat at the policy table.

"We see Sherrod Brown winning in Ohio as damaging the crypto industry's political clout as the industry worked to defeat him," Jaret Seiberg, TD Cowen's Washington analyst, said in a note Wednesday. "We did not think Clarity could advance over the next two years. This makes us more confident in our prediction."

The crypto industry spent more than $200 million to sway the midterms, hoping to get leaders elected that could push a comprehensive crypto market structure bill over the finish line after the Clarity Act stalled in the Senate.

Seiberg emphasized that Democrats "will investigate Trump's crypto entanglements including World Liberty Financial" and said "the resulting political environment may make it impossible to advance a version of Clarity that the crypto sector could back."

Mike Townsend, Charles Schwab's managing director of legislative and regulatory affairs, said he expects "Democrats to push next year for a version of the bill that is much tougher on cryptocurrency companies."

The stakes extend beyond market structure legislation via Clarity. Stablecoin innovation; decentralized finance, or DeFi, development; banking access; tokenization; and sensible tax policy are priorities the industry sees as important to ensuring the U.S. remains competitive in the global crypto economy.

The industry will need continued bipartisan engagement to ensure these priorities aren't sidelined by changing political dynamics. And Democrats have historically been less supportive of crypto than Republicans, though that divide has narrowed as more Democrats embrace the industry.

The implications of Democrats' big win aren't all bad. Crypto has reached a level of financial integration that could be difficult to reverse, with its future increasingly centered on establishing crypto as financial infrastructure. Even with the Clarity Act potentially stalled until 2028, key financial regulators can help advance the industry through rule-making.

Coinbase's vice president of U.S. policy, Kara Calvert, points out that the election results point to a historic shift in the makeup of the incoming Congress, with a record number of pro-crypto voices expected to join its ranks.

"With last night's results, the 120th Congress is on track to have more new pro-crypto members than we've ever seen in any freshman class," she said. "Crypto is 100% bipartisan, and that's why the future of finance does not rest on either political party or a single election night. Democrats and Republicans alike know that clear rules protect consumers and keep innovation in the U.S."

As of Thursday morning, 19 candidates characterized as pro crypto by the advocacy nonprofit Stand With Crypto have been elected to the Senate versus eight Senate candidates it characterizes as anti crypto. In the House, 228 pro-crypto candidates have been elected versus 106 the group deems anti crypto.

Several races have not been called, but Fairshake — the super PAC launched in 2023 to support pro-crypto candidates regardless of party — has so far won 29 of the 34 races it spent on, per Reuters, including three of the six House candidates it prioritized by spending a baseline of $1 million on their campaigns.

Dante Disparte, chief strategy officer and head of global policy and operations at Circle, emphasized Circle's bipartisan approach and readiness for new Senate and House leadership, but said it "may take longer to get Clarity tabled again."

That bipartisan support may offer a blueprint for what comes next, but even if crypto legislation stalls, progress can continue, said Joseph Chalom, CEO of ether treasury company Sharplink.

"We expect the Clarity Act to remain on hold through 2028. Even so, there is a clear path forward for stablecoins … and for the tokenization of public equities under the SEC's five-year innovation exemption," he said. "Technological progress is rarely rolled back. Once the benefits of faster settlement, lower costs and markets that never close become clear to investors and institutions, this shift will be very difficult to reverse, regardless of who wins the White House in 2028."

Near-term, investors should expect more volatility as the market tries to figure out how crypto regulation may shift under a Democratic Congress.

The impact of the blue wave "should vary considerably across assets," said James Butterfill, head of research at CoinShares. "We would expect U.S. crypto equities to be more sensitive than bitcoin, particularly businesses reliant on new regulatory permissions. Established, compliant operators could even benefit from greater scrutiny of competitors. So miners who already have data centers set up are likely to remain in high demand by AI hyperscalers."

— CNBC's Talia Kaplan contributed reporting.

#2885. CNBC's experts on whether the AI trade is ending and what investors should do next

Amid a powerful rout in tech stocks, investors told CNBC on Thursday that something may be fundamentally breaking in the AI trade following the big success of Democrats in Tuesday's midterm elections and the threat they try to slow the data center buildout.

Democrats are more aggressively anti-data center than Republicans, and Wall Street is quickly redoing its math what any restrictions they implement could mean for the related companies' future growth.

"Right now, investors are questioning that $1.2 trillion of capex that we forecast for next year," Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer at One Point BFG Wealth Partners, told CNBC. "Well, maybe that's not going to happen."

Boockvar believes this could be the start of the end of the AI trade as we know it.

Whether it's completely over or not, investors need to be reassessing how they're planning to play the AI trade going forward, the analysts said.

The Nasdaq Composite dropped 5% on Thursday and fell into correction territory, off by more than 11% from its record high set last month. The iShares Semiconductor ETF dropped 11% on Thursday, its biggest decline since during the Covid breakout in March 2020. The Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF (AIQ) is down 6% on the day and down 15% over the past month.

"There has been a huge change in the outlook for AI infrastructure buildout," Eric Johnston, head of equities at Cantor Fitzgerald, told CNBC. "The entire economy and the consumer and earnings growth are all levered to that buildout."

The selling Thursday spilled over to non-AI stocks with the Dow Jones Industrial average down more than 1,600 points.

Josh Brown pointed to the 4.8% yield for the 10-year Treasury yield, saying a compelling risk-free rate is causing investors to reconsider taking the risk in these volatile AI stocks.

"You don't need to be at 80% U.S. stocks and have 60% of that exposure be tech," Brown said.

Many investors believe the AI trade isn't over completely, investors just need to get more selective.

"The AI buildout just got harder," said Rob Sechan, Newedge Capital Group Founder & Managing Partner:

"Nobody voted to make compute less scarce," Sechan said, citing Microsoft's Azure cloud business growing 48% year over year in its most recent third quarter. That level of growth suggests its capacity constrained, not demand constrained, he said.

"When new capacity gets harder to build, existing capacity becomes more valuable," Sechan said.

Richard Clode, portfolio manager at Janus Henderson, noted a few bright spots in tech on Thursday despite the highly correlated downward movements in the big tech indices.

"Motorola Solutions had some good results," he said. "We're seeing a little bit of rotation into some of the … internet names...Sony reported some good results, and again they were up strongly overnight."

"So there are some brief pockets of respite from this, but obviously pretty painful across the board today," he said.

Some experts believe the selling was overdone and investors could start nibbling.

This "indiscriminate selling" is a "buying opportunity," said Larry Adam, Raymond James chief investment officer. If investors "take a longer term perspective, which is what we do, I think the valuations at today's levels will tend to prove to be a good buying opportunity," he said, urging investors to look at the fundamentals.

Victoria Greene, chief investment officer of G Squared Private Wealth, said she saw some strong supports around the S&P 500's 200-day moving average and was on the lookout for a market bounce following Thursday's rout.

"Typically, the average return is plus about 180 basis points the next day," she said. "The question we have to ask ourselves: Is this a pullback in an uptrend, which is what I believe? Or is this the end-all, be-all [and] the wheels are coming off and everybody just needs to buy T-bills? I don't think we're there yet."

#2882. Derrick Henry's production has plummeted without Lamar Jackson this season

Without quarterback Lamar Jackson, the Ravens want to be able to rely on running back Derrick Henry. That plan isn't working.

In Thursday night's 33-10 loss to the Jaguars, Henry managed just 57 yards on 17 carries. That continues what has been happening all season, with Henry struggling to get anything going without Jackson on the field.

It was a bad omen in Week 4 against the Titans, when Jackson left at halftime with an ankle injury and Henry was ineffective in the second half. In the first half of that game, with Jackson on the field, Henry had seven carries for 38 yards, an average of 5.4 yards per carry, and a touchdown. In the second half with Tyler Huntley, Henry had 16 carries for 35 yards, an average of 2.2 yards per carry, and no touchdowns.

Jackson has played one snap since that Titans game, and the story has been the same, with Henry not able to do much of anything.

Overall this season, in three and a half games playing with Jackson, Henry has 73 carries for 339 yards, an average of 4.6 yards per carry and 97 yards per game, and seven touchdowns. In five and a half games without Jackson, Henry has 102 carries for 350 yards, an average of 3.4 yards per carry and 64 yards per game, and one touchdown.

At 4-5 and in last place in the AFC North, the Ravens, who entered the year with Super Bowl aspirations, are on the verge of their season collapsing. They need to turn things around, and they need Henry to turn things around.

#2879. Moritz Seider Sounds Like a Captain With Powerful Message After Red Wings Loss

The Detroit Red Wings were less than two minutes away from earning at least one point against the Vegas Golden Knights on Thursday night. Instead, another late-game breakdown left them empty-handed, and Moritz Seider wasn't interested in making excuses.

Following Detroit's heartbreaking 2-1 loss at Little Caesars Arena, the 25-year-old defenseman delivered a blunt message about what needs to change.

And considering the growing conversation surrounding Detroit's vacant captaincy, his words carried additional weight.

Nov 3, 2026; Tampa, Florida, USA; Detroit Red Wings defenseman Moritz Seider (53) plays the puck during the third period against Tampa Bay Lightning at Benchmark International Arena. Mandatory Credit: Pablo Robles-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

The Red Wings battled one of the NHL's strongest teams for nearly 60 minutes, but Trevor Connelly's goal with just 1:42 remaining in regulation handed Vegas the victory.

When asked what Detroit needs to improve in late-game situations, Seider delivered the following message in his postgame comments:

"We just got to be better. I think that's pretty simple. There are many aspects of the game that we need to focus on, but I think we just got to be real present in the moment and just have got to want it more than the other team."

Seider wasn't pointing fingers at a particular teammate or suggesting Detroit had played poorly all night. Instead, he was emphasizing the urgency and focus required to finish close games against quality opponents.

It's a message the Red Wings desperately need to hear.

Detroit had plenty of reasons to believe Thursday would end differently.

Daniil Tarasov delivered an outstanding performance, stopping 32 shots, including 14 in the opening period. Meanwhile, Anton Johansson gave the Red Wings a 1-0 lead early in the third period with his second goal of the season.

Unfortunately, that advantage disappeared just over two minutes later when Braeden Bowman tied the game for Vegas.

The score remained deadlocked until Connelly beat Tarasov in the closing minutes.

According to the NHL's official game recap, the winning goal developed when Connelly received a pass from Jack Eichel, used a toe-drag to create shooting space, and beat Tarasov with a wrist shot.

Head coach Todd McLellan acknowledged that Detroit had competed well enough to give itself an opportunity. But one late mistake ultimately decided a game that could have gone either way.

And that's precisely what makes Seider's comments important.

Detroit doesn't necessarily need to dominate every opponent for 60 minutes. It needs to execute when the game is on the line.

The timing of Seider's comments is particularly interesting because Red Wings fans have spent the past several days discussing whether he should become Detroit's next captain.

On Thursday morning, an unusual practice video sparked speculation that Seider could be receiving the captaincy.

Players reportedly waited several minutes for Seider before beginning drills, leading some fans to wonder whether something significant had happened inside the locker room.

There has been no official announcement, but Seider continues to demonstrate the qualities associated with a team captain.

He's willing to speak candidly after difficult losses, take responsibility for the team's shortcomings, and challenge his teammates to improve.

As we previously examined when discussing Detroit's captaincy decision, Seider has already established himself as one of the organization's most natural leadership candidates.

Thursday's comments only strengthen that argument.

Detroit now sits at 7-7-3 with 17 points, having lost two consecutive games and three of its past four.

The Red Wings will begin a four-game road trip Saturday against the Colorado Avalanche, giving them an immediate opportunity to respond to Thursday's disappointment.

But the bigger issue goes beyond one loss.

Detroit has repeatedly shown it can compete with quality opponents. The challenge is turning those competitive performances into victories.

My take: Seider's message is exactly what this team needs right now.

He's not asking teammates to perform miracles or pretending that Detroit can eliminate every mistake. He's demanding better execution, greater focus, and a stronger commitment when the outcome hangs in the balance.

Those are reasonable expectations for a team trying to establish itself as a legitimate playoff contender.

And whether or not Seider eventually receives the "C," he's already speaking like someone who understands the responsibility that comes with wearing it.

Now the Red Wings need to show they're listening.

#2877. What are the best NFL trade deadline deals ever? These 9 top the list

As the 2026 NFL trade deadline approaches, many top contenders hope to make a midseason acquisition that pushes them toward a Super Bowl title. Historically, only a few trades have turned out as impactful as a team hoped. Fewer still have aged particularly well in the years since the moves were made.

Given the brevity of the season, the time necessary to get players acclimated to a new team's schemes, and a salary cap to deal with, the NFL trade deadline is not quite as active as that of other sports. Only in the last decade or so has it become really significant, with more teams hitting the gas on mid-season deals since 2016.

As such, most of the best trade deadline deals in history have come since the turn of the century. These nine moves in particular stand out for the impact each player made with the team that acquired them:

NFL TRADE DEADLINE: Will the Jets spring another November surprise?

When Kyle Shanahan took over as the San Francisco 49ers' head coach before the 2017 season, he came with plans to overhaul the team's offensive scheme. Then-starter Colin Kaepernick was not an apparent fit for his offense, so Shanahan allowed Kaepernick to walk, hoping to bring in a new starting quarterback to slot into his offense.

The 49ers head coach found his man in a trade deadline deal to acquire Jimmy Garoppolo from the New England Patriots. It cost the 49ers their 2018 second-round pick, but the trade ended up being the spark the team needed that year.

Garoppolo made his debut for his new team in Week 12 following a lower-body injury to starter C.J. Beathard, and he became the team's starter the following week. Garoppolo led the 49ers to five straight wins to close the season after starting the year 1-10.

That February, San Francisco extended Garoppolo on a five-year deal.

"Jimmy G" had his ups and downs with the Niners, but the team made the playoffs in three of his six seasons – including its first Super Bowl appearance since 2012 in 2019. He also has the fourth-best win percentage (.691) by a San Francisco quarterback in franchise history, behind Steve Young, Joe Montana and current starter Brock Purdy.

The 2018 first-round pick led the Chicago Bears in tackles in the four full years he played for the team. In 2020 and 2021, he earned second-team All-Pro nods after finishing in the top six in combined tackles each year.

The writing was on the wall for Smith's time in Chicago when the team couldn't reach an agreement with the linebacker ahead of his fifth season. He requested a trade in August 2022 and told the media he didn't feel properly valued by the new front office regime that took over that January.

After eight games, the Baltimore Ravens traded 2023 second- and fifth-round picks to the Bears for Smith. He finished the year with a career-high 169 tackles across two teams, 4.5 sacks, 11 tackles for a loss, and six passes defended. That production earned him first-team All-Pro honors for the first time in his career.

Smith got a first-team All-Pro nod for a second straight time in 2023 with his 158 tackles – including 21 in a single game – plus 1.5 sacks, five tackles for a loss, eight passes defended, and a forced fumble.

This trade has continued to age even better as Smith re-affirms year after year that he's one of the league's best all-around inside linebackers. He earned his third first-team All-Pro nod in a row in 2024 with 154 tackles, 1.5 sacks, four tackles for a loss, four passes defended, and a forced fumble.

Even though Smith did not earn All-Pro honors again in 2025, he was named a Pro Bowler for the fourth time in his career. Four years later, the trade has still been a big win for the Ravens, who signed him to a five-year, $100 million extension in January 2023.

NFL TRADE DEADLINE: From the Bills to 49ers, 1 trade target for each division leader

The Pittsburgh Steelers' acquisition of Fitzpatrick was similar to the Ravens' trade for Smith. The main difference was that this mid-season trade was less of a trade deadline move; it happened six weeks before the cut-off in 2019.

Fitzpatrick requested a trade one week into the safety's second season with the Miami Dolphins. The 2018 first-round pick felt the coaching staff in Miami was not utilizing his skill set correctly. He made 12 tackles across two games before the Dolphins and Steelers completed their trade.

In September 2019, Pittsburgh sent its 2020 first- and fifth-round picks and a 2021 sixth-round pick in exchange for Fitzpatrick, Miami's 2020 fourth-round pick and 2021 seventh-round pick. Fitzpatrick made his Steelers debut in Week 3 and established himself as one of the league's best safeties by the end of the year.

He was a first-team All-Pro safety in 2019 and again in 2020. Fitzpatrick earned a third such nod in four years with more first-team All-Pro honors in 2022. It was a year in which he tallied six interceptions that tied for the league lead. He has five Pro Bowl appearances in 2019, 2020, 2022, 2023 and 2024.

The Steelers traded Fitzpatrick back to Miami before the 2025 season, but his years in Pittsburgh remain the most decorated of his career.

When Jon Gruden took over as head coach of the Raiders in 2018, it didn't take him long to make some big moves that flipped productive players for draft picks. Just ahead of that 2018 season, the then-Oakland Raiders traded star edge rusher Khalil Mack and two draft picks to the Chicago Bears for a return of four picks - including two first-rounders.

After a 1-5 start to the 2018 season, Gruden denied rumors that he was seeking trade partners for Amari Cooper, who was the Raiders' No. 1 receiver in each of his first three pro seasons. Nevertheless, the Raiders traded the wideout for the Dallas Cowboys' 2019 first-round pick in late October.

When he arrived in Dallas, Cooper didn't take long to re-establish his reliability as a top receiving option. Despite playing just nine games for the Cowboys in 2018, the Alabama product's 725 receiving yards, including a 180-yard performance against Washington and a 217-yard day against Philadelphia and six touchdowns, led the entire team that year.

Cooper's three and a half years with the Cowboys were the most productive of his career. Before Dallas traded him in 2022, he had accumulated 3,893 receiving yards and tallied 27 touchdowns on 292 catches – his best numbers for a single team across the four he's played for.

Although the Cowboys never made a deep playoff run while Cooper was on the team, he was a crucial part of the Dallas offense in all four of his seasons.

Spoiler alert: this is the only trade before 2000 to make this list. Herschel Walker will make the worst trade list; Vikings fans, don't worry.

Dickerson entered his fifth season with the Rams having led the NFL in rushing yards in three of his first four seasons. One of those seasons was his record-setting 2,105-yard 1984, which also included a league-leading 14 touchdowns. Shortly after setting the single-season rushing record – one that still stands – negotiations on an extension broke down.

Three games into the strike-shortened 1987 season, Los Angeles shipped Dickerson to Indianapolis as part of a three-team, 10-player trade. The move was somewhat ironic – four years earlier, Dickerson had made it known before the draft he would refuse to play for the then-Baltimore-based franchise.

In just nine games with the Colts that year, Dickerson tallied 1,011 yards and five touchdowns. He earned his fourth Pro Bowl nod and was named to the All-Pro first team for the fourth time. Indianapolis made the playoffs in 1987, going 9-6 and winning the AFC East one year after going 3-13.

The next year, Dickerson once again led the NFL with 1,659 rushing yards and 2,036 yards from scrimmage. He earned a fifth career Pro Bowl and All-Pro first team nod, but the Colts missed the playoffs.

After a 1989 season that included 1,311 rushing yards and a sixth career Pro Bowl nod (but no playoff berth), Dickerson's final two seasons in Indy were less smooth. The Colts traded him to the Raiders in 1992, ending his tenure.

Jalen Ramsey quickly established himself as a star NFL cornerback. He was the Defensive Rookie of the Year runner-up to Joey Bosa in 2016 and earned his initial first-team All-Pro recognition in his second season in 2017.

If winning cures everything, losing exposes issues. The Jacksonville Jaguars' AFC championship game run in 2017 was followed by a 5-11 season in 2018. Then, Jacksonville began the 2019 season 0-2.

During the Jaguars' Week 2 loss, Ramsey had a verbal altercation with then-head coach Doug Marrone that escalated to the point that both had to be physically restrained. The next week, the cornerback played his final game with Jacksonville.

In mid-October, the Jaguars traded Ramsey to the Los Angeles Rams for two first-round picks and a 2021 fourth-rounder.

The cornerback was a Pro Bowler in his four seasons in Los Angeles and earned two more first-team All-Pro nods in 2020 and 2021. Ramsey helped the Rams win a Super Bowl in the 2021 season, accumulating 13 total tackles and four passes defended throughout the playoff run, including one pass defense in the Super Bowl.

The Broncos scuffled for years after Miller won Super Bowl 50 MVP. Their only winning season after that magical 2015 was in the year after – a 9-7 record with no playoff berth in 2016.

In 2021, Denver started 3-0 before losing four straight. As part of their efforts to escape the multi-year slide, new general manager George Paton sent their former Super Bowl MVP to the Rams for second- and third-round picks.

In eight games with Los Angeles, Miller recorded five sacks, one pass defense, a forced fumble and 12 tackles for a loss. The Rams lost three straight games after the trade deadline, but their five-game win streak that followed had them in position to win the NFC West with a win or a Cardinals loss in Week 18. Arizona obliged.

Miller played in all four of Los Angeles's playoff games and led all defenders in that postseason with four sacks and six tackles for a loss.

The Rams went on to win the Super Bowl over the Bengals in February 2022. Miller had two sacks in the game, getting him to 4.5 Super Bowl sacks in his career. That tied him with Charles Haley for most sacks by a single player in Super Bowl history – a record he and Haley still share.

When healthy, Christian McCaffrey was one of the best offensive players in the NFL with the Carolina Panthers.

In 2019, his third season in the NFL, the former Stanford Cardinal led the league with 403 touches, 2,392 scrimmage yards, and 19 total touchdowns. He earned first-team All-Pro recognition for the first time, his first Pro Bowl nod, and a third-place finish in Offensive Player of the Year voting.

Unfortunately, for the running back and the Panthers, McCaffrey couldn't stay healthy for the two years after. He played just ten games in the 2020 and 2021 seasons, accumulating 212 touches, 1,159 yards from scrimmage, and eight touchdowns.

With Carolina's window of contention closing, the Panthers decided to flip the star tailback for future draft picks halfway through the 2022 season. The 49ers, looking to make a postseason push, gave up their second, third, and fourth-round picks in 2023 and a 2024 fifth-round pick.

In 11 games for San Francisco, McCaffrey led the team with 746 rushing yards and six rushing touchdowns. He was also the fourth-most productive pass-catcher on the 49ers that year, with 52 catches for 464 receiving yards.

The 2023 season was even better. He led the league with 1,459 rushing yards, 2,023 scrimmage yards, and 21 total touchdowns. In 2023, McCaffrey earned his third Pro Bowl nod, second first-team All-Pro honors, an Offensive Player of the Year win, and third-place finish in MVP voting.

The running back's stellar year was a big reason the 49ers made it to Super Bowl 58. He became the first player in Super Bowl history with 75 rushing and 75 receiving yards in the game.

More injuries minimized McCaffrey's impact in 2024, but his 2025 season was a return to form. He finished with 2,126 scrimmage yards on a league-leading 413 touchdowns and earned first-team All-Pro honors for the third time in his career. He also won Comeback Player of the Year, finished second in Offensive Player of the Year voting and was fourth in MVP voting.

Lynch had a strong first two seasons as a pro in 2007 and 2008. He put up back-to-back 1,000-yard seasons with 15 total touchdowns across those two years and a Pro Bowl nod in 2008.

Before the 2009 season, Lynch was arrested on misdemeanor weapons charges that led to a three-game suspension to start the year. That season was also the year that Fred Jackson supplanted Lynch as the Buffalo Bills' starting back en route to his first 1,000-yard season.

Lynch played just four more games for the Bills in the 2010 season before the Seattle Seahawks traded a 2011 fourth-round pick and a 2012 conditional fifth-round pick for the running back. The rest is history.

Seattle's new acquisition established an early legacy in the Seahawks franchise, with a 67-yard touchdown run featuring nine broken tackles against the New Orleans Saints - dubbed the "Beast Quake" - in the 2010 playoffs.

#2871. Joe Brady on cutting S C.J. Gardner-Johnson: "It was the best interests of the football team"

On the day the NFL suspended former Bills safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson for spitting on an opponent, Buffalo coach Joe Brady said the team would not be cutting Gardner-Johnson. After the game that Gardner-Johnson missed, the Bills cut him.

Meeting with reporters on Thursday, Brady explained the reversal.

“There was a lot to evaluate,” Brady said. “You know, we got together and figured out, ‘Hey, this is what we felt like this was the best thing to do for the Buffalo Bills.’ I have so much love for [C.J.]. Like, I really do. I loved getting to coach him. I loved being around him. I loved — I did love the edge, and his personality allowing him to be him, right?, and as a person. So that didn’t make the decision easy at all.

“But we also have to be an organization that, you know, it’s unfortunate obviously what happened, you know? But it also opened a door and an opportunity for guys the other day, and that was a part of evaluation. And seeing how those guys kind of played, and you know with a lot of the roster moves. And, again, this wasn’t — we didn’t come out of the game post Vegas and say, ‘This is what we were going to do. We’re just gonna do this the following Monday.’ We were, you know, the plan was him being here and we were going to evaluate it after the game in Baltimore. And we felt like with some of the moving parts we had to do it was the best interests of the football team.”

Gardner-Johnson’s suspension opened the door for Damar Hamlin to start the game against the Ravens. And Hamlin apparently did well enough to help the Bills realize that, all things considered, the “best interests” of the Bills meant the Bills were better off without the “high maintenance” Gardner-Johnson.

#2870. Five Plays: Stanford Third Quarter

It took until the second half, but Louisville started to get more aggressive with their linebackers. On this play, Stanquan Clark times up the snap before shooting the gap to make a play in the backfield. He's just unlucky because the play goes to the other side, which leaves him grasping for air.

Stanford uses motion again on this play with a full shift of their tight ends across the field. Louisville tracks the motion, but you will notice that no one picks up the running back coming out of the backfield. So, on this play, Stanford takes advantage of two different issues UofL had in coverage earlier in the game. They don't identify their responsibility after the motion, and they don't account for the running back out of the backfield on a short-yardage pass.

This is a nice play design and call by Stanford, but it would be nice to be able to say that the play just beat Louisville as opposed to the defense not even giving itself a chance.

Lincoln Kienholz had his weekly instalment of "Man, it's nice to have a quarterback who can do this" in the second quarter with his arm, but he does it with his legs on this play. I especially love the spin move that wasn't really needed.

I wrote about Louisville needing to attack the edges of Stanford's defense in the What To Watch For post last week, so I was really happy to see them try to get outside a lot in this game. The first drive of the game was edge runs and swing passes, and they came back to it in the third quarter for this nice touchdown.

As good as Isaac Brown is in space, he should buy dinner for Jaleel Skinner and TJ McWilliams for their blocking on this play. McWilliams is the outside receiver to the top of the screen. He gets up to the outside linebacker, who is flowing towards him before passing him off to Skinner, who gets outside after going in motion. McWilliams then moves up to the cornerback to create a tunnel for Isaac to run through. This is teach tape.

I'm a bit of a broken record on this, but I don't really understand why they can run this defense as often as they run Cover 3. Situations will dictate a lot of things, but the only real difference is that they are a little more spread out. But if this were first down, you would not be blitzing Kaleb Perry, who loops around on a stunt on this play. He would be right in the middle of the field to play the run. Ben Perry would also not be in press coverage in the slot. He would be backed off a bit and could react to a run play.

If they were playing well in zone coverage, this wouldn't be a problem, but at this point in the season I can't understand why they haven't adjusted.

This was one of the dumbest calls I've seen in all the years I've been doing these film reviews. Stanford had just scored on the previous drive, and they had already shown that they could get explosive passing plays and chunk runs against this defense. A screen pass or a draw play to try to get a cheap first down makes much more sense here. Instead, they give the Cards an opportunity to get a true momentum-shifting play for a defense that had been gashed all day.

It was really great to see everyone on defense make the right play here. Perry closes on the initial receiver, while TJ Capers immediately reacts to the pitch and makes a big hit on the receiver even though he didn't make the catch. Tayon Holloway looks like he's running a scoop-and-score drill, too. It looks easy, but picking up a fumble on the run like this gets bungled a lot. He does well to bend his knees and drop his butt, which is where a lot of guys get it wrong. They keep running while trying to grab the ball in stride. Secure the ball, then take off.

Jabari Mack is good for one or two good plays a game, and this was a really good one. He is in man coverage on this play, but because he opens his hips at the beginning of the play, he is able to keep up with his man while also having an eye in the backfield. When Davis Warren commits to throwing the wheel route here, Mack breaks off of his man to get over the top and pick off the pass.

This was also a really nice catch for a defensive back. He high-points the ball over the receiver, who is in position to catch the ball. Mack snatches it away before it hits the receiver's hands.

Louisville attacks the edge again, and Isaac Brown just does what he does. There are maybe five guys in the country who could score on this play, and it's always nice to have one of those few.

#2868. Lakers vs. Blazers Preview: It’s payback time

The Lakers (7-2) are back home, where they will host a rematch with the Portland Trail Blazers (6-1) on Friday. The matchup will also serve as an NBA Cup contest, with both teams competing in West Group C.

Who: Los Angeles Lakers vs. Portland Trail Blazers

One of the Lakers' two losses this season came at the hands of the Trail Blazers, who ran the purple and gold off their home floor last week. That was the same game that exposed the Lakers' early flaws such as their inability to rebound the ball well, over reliance on Luka Dončić and overall team defense. While those weaknesses are still apparent, the Lakers have done a better job of navigating them and responding since that loss.

On Friday, they have the chance to get even.

This will be a good opportunity to see whether the Lakers have learned from their loss, how they've adjusted and how determined they are to make a run in the NBA Cup after losing pretty badly in the opener against the Warriors.

Here are three storylines worth noting ahead of the matchup between the Lakers and Blazers:

Morant was a huge factor in the Blazers' first victory over the Lakers, posting 23 points. He easily got in the paint and scored nine out of his 13 attempts. It felt like the Lakers had no answer for him. Fortunately for the purple and gold, they won't have to think about Ja on Friday because he's currently recovering from a Grade 2 hamstring injury.

Instead, the Lakers should expect more touches for Deni Avdija, Damian Lillard and Scoot Henderson, who replaced Morant in the starting lineup.

Defense will be the biggest key for the Lakers if they want to come away with a win. In their previous meeting, Los Angeles allowed Portland to shoot 50% from beyond the arc while giving up 56 points in the paint. The Blazers' hot shooting may have been an outlier but there's no guarantee it won't happen again if the Lakers don't tighten things up defensively. The Blazers have enough scoring to match the Lakers' firepower.

Portland is the seventh-best rebounding team in the league and currently has a top-10 offensive and defensive rating. They lead the league in points per game (121.9), which is why they're a tough cover. This isn't one of those teams the Lakers can just overwhelm with Dončić's brilliance and talent alone. They'll have to work on both ends of the floor.

If their first NBA Cup match was any indication, the Lakers didn't seem too interested in making a statement, which is unfortunate because these games are so much fun to win. Hopefully that changes for this one because it's pretty much a do-or-die game for the Lakers if they want to stay alive in the NBA Cup. Not only are they 0-1, they have a concerning -17 point differential and, if they want to increase their chances of advancing, they're going to need to win in some blow outs.

It's a tough task but one the purple and gold should aim to do if they truly want to exact revenge against the Blazers on Friday.

The Lakers and Warriors are the only ones in West Group C that have played in the NBA Cup so far, but expect the standings to change on Friday when the Spurs and Kings go at it.

For the Lakers' injury report, Sandro Mamukelashvili (illness) is listed as questionable.

Bronny James Jr., (G-League) and Cameron Carr (G-League) will be with the Coachella Valley Lakers.

As for the Blazers, Vit Krejci (left ankle fracture), Ja Morant (left hamstring strain) and Shaedon Sharpe (right meniscus surgery) are out.

After three losses to the same man, Yodphupa Petkiatpet finally flipped the script on longtime rival Komawut FA Group, edging him by split decision. The 22-year-old was determined to settle the score, which included a razor-close split decision at ONE Friday Fights 50 in 2024.

From the opening bell, Komawut marched forward hunting the one shot that would end it early, throwing haymakers while the clinch specialist added punishment from the inside. Like a man on a mission, the Kiwi closed in and went for the finish. A stabbing teep to the body ended it at 1:27 of round three, and the Tihipuke Muay Thai affiliate walked onto the main roster with his pristine 24-0 record intact.

Over in flyweight Muay Thai, Egypt's Tantawy Ahmed "Elgalad" made it three successive wins on the global stage, putting on a kicking clinic for a unanimous decision over Kongchai Chanaidonmueang. A massive head kick knockdown sealed the win and moved the Egyptian to 24-7.

Serving as the night's opening act, Thai veteran Dabdam Por Tor Tor Thongtawee sent Englishman Cal Cook to the canvas twice en route to the unanimous decision win in strawweight Muay Thai. The result lifted him to 70-30.

#2864. Rashee Rice files for bankruptcy, citing more than $3.45 million in debt

Chiefs receiver Rashee Rice is in the final year of his four-year, $6.45 million rookie contract. He nevertheless has far greater liabilities than assets. And he’s looking to wipe the slate clean as to at least some of them.

Via ESPN, Rice has filed for federal bankruptcy protection.

The filing cites more than $3.45 million in debts, with $2.1 million of it tied to multiple plaintiffs in the accident caused by his street-racing incident in early 2024.

Rice has yet to get a second contract. He’s due to become a free agent in March, and he has played well enough to get signed, by the Chiefs or someone else.

By then, Rice should have more than enough money to pay all of his debts without relying on the ability to activate Chapter 7 of the bankruptcy laws to discharge some or many of them for cents on the dollar.

That could be the first argument made by his creditors. Given Rice’s earning potential, it’s just a matter of time before he has the money needed to pay all of his bills and settle all of his debts.

#2859. Here’s where the Steelers’ defense still has room to grow

It's a good time to be a Steelers fan. Pittsburgh sits atop the AFC North entering a Week 9 bye, coming off a big win over the rival Cleveland Browns where the Steelers both scored a lot of points (27) and didn't give up many (six).

As a result, you're going to see a lot of positive Steelers coverage over the next two weeks. And for good reason. The team's running game and front seven were undoubtedly elite against Cleveland. Pittsburgh has been playing like one of the NFL's best teams as of the late.

But as knowledgeable NFL writers/podcasters Jon Ledyard and Derrick Bell quipped following the Browns game, a lot is going right for the Steelers, "but the forward pass, especially on offense, still stands between them and greatness."

Most are aware of the Steelers' passing deficiencies on offense, but I'd argue that on the other side of the ball, Pittsburgh's passing defense could be a similarly limiting factor on the team's long-term potential.

Pittsburgh's safety room has been an apparent issue since before the season started, and even with Robert Spears-Jennings blowing past Year 1 expectations as a seventh-round rookie, the play at the position has been a weaker spot on defense. DeShon Elliott missed much of the early season with injury and hasn't been that impactful since returning, while free agent signing Jaquan Brisker hasn't always been able to rise to the challenge when it comes to coverage ability and instincts.

Meanwhile at cornerback, the group's injury issues have largely subsided at this point in the season. But with Joey Porter Jr. — by far the best player in the secondary — never suiting up for the black and gold before being traded to Dallas, an expected strength on defense has turned into a position that's been solid at best in 2026.

All of that's to say, despite Pittsburgh having not allowed 20 points in each of its last three games, the "elite" label the defense has earned as of late doesn't feel accurate to the state of the secondary, which looks like a potentially ticking time bomb with Joe Burrow, CJ Stroud and Trevor Lawrence still waiting on the schedule.

Pittsburgh's season defensive stats match the eye test. While ranking near the top of the league in stopping the run (third), sacking the quarterback (first), and forcing a quick time to throw (third — partially explaining a surprisingly middling pressure rate), the Steelers are middle of the pack when stopping the pass (17th) and among the worst in yards after catch allowed (30th) and average separation allowed per target (32nd).

The dichotomy was obvious in Pittsburgh's recent big win over Cleveland, where the Steelers' front seven dominated to the tune of eight team sacks and only 34 rushing yards allowed, holding the Browns to single-digit points. However, Browns quarterback DeShaun Watson passed for 324 yards — and while it's more than fair to point out that Cleveland was in a must-pass situation for much of the game and against a prevent-oriented Steelers defense late, the Browns also missed a number of open passing opportunities that would've juiced Watson's numbers even more.

Essentially, in the rare instances when the Steelers' pass rush wasn't completely dominating on Sunday, the Pittsburgh secondary wasn't exactly holding up its end of the bargain.

Here are some of the bigger plays the Steelers gave up in the passing game on Sunday:

In the first clip above, Brisker just gets beat, plain and simple, when manned up against a good receiving tight end in the Browns' Harold Fannin Jr. On the second, the Browns find the open space in the Steelers' two-high coverage, with Brisker stuck in no man's land between the running back and the corner route. In the final clip, there's a miscommunication between Daylen Everette and Asante Samuel Jr., with both jumping the same route as KC Concepcion scoots by both for a 20-plus-yard gain.

To be fair, only the last play is a true breakdown in coverage, with the first two being the sort of man- and zone-beaters you expect to see work at some point in an NFL game (even if you would hope Brisker holds up better against tight ends in coverage).

In the first clip above, Samuel loses Jerry Jeudy (bottom of the screen wide receiver) in coverage; the Browns receiver was open for a 70-yard touchdown well before Watson threw the ball. Instead, the play goes for just a first down to Fannin.

On the next play, the Browns run a play-action concept, and with both safeties preoccupied by the deep route, Samuel is left to choose between covering Denzel Boston and going after Watson. He never really commits to either, and is saved by a terrible throw by Watson. It negates what would've been a 20- or 30-yard gain.

The next play is much tighter coverage and a bit more nit-picky than the other examples in this article, but Boston clearly gets a step on Jamel Dean with the Steelers in quarters. Brisker stops his feet and leaves the corner on an island, losing inside leverage. A good throw closer to the post is a touchdown.

Finally, there's a late-game extended play where Jeudy once again finds himself open, with no Steelers defender within five yards of him in any direction. Watson steps up in the pocket, draws Jeudy even more open, and then checks it down to the running back — who still gets the first down.

Of course, you can go back and watch any good NFL defensive performance and find open players who were missed. However, I'd argue there were a lot more than usual in the Steelers' Sunday win.

But there's also another level of nuance: It was a good gameplan by the Steelers, who knew they could beat the Browns with pressure, unleashing their second-highest single-game blitz rate of the season thus far (30%). Watson, who has actually had a solid 2026, looked uncomfortable and inaccurate all game. The Steelers' front seven feasted, the secondary benefited from off-target throws, and Pittsburgh didn't give up a touchdown in a three-score win.

Honestly, my thoughts in this article can best be summed up by the below play, where Robert Spears-Jennings jumps Denzel Boston's route, throwing Watson out of rhythm and into an eventual sack. With no coverage help behind Spears-Jennings, Boston was left wide open — but the aggression, paired with pressure, resulted in a positive play for the Steelers.

However, it won't always be that easy — especially later in the season and postseason against better quarterbacks and passing offenses (Frankly, besides Burrow and Drake Maye, have the Steelers faced many good passers this year?). The Steelers' pass defense as a whole has been adequate this season, but it hasn't been at the level the team's overall defensive numbers would indicate. Whether it's athleticism in man defense or chemistry in zone, there's still a lot of work to do.

But it still does feel like an improved Steelers defense than in past seasons. The pass rush has been revitalized, and as evidenced by the Browns game, that can cover for a number of sins on the back end. And the Steelers have two rookies in Robert Spears-Jennings and Daylen Everette who should only continue to develop and improve the secondary with time.

In the short term, the Steelers also have an entire bye week to aid their preparation ahead of a rematch with a high-flying Bengals passing game in Week 10. The Steelers' secondary has some notable issues, but it's far too early to call it a season killer.

#2858. Game Recap: Booker drops 30 as Suns secure win over Magic, 117-104

It was a much-needed victory for the Suns tonight as they improved to 2-5 on the season.

Phoenix spotted Orlando an early lead, then took the game over with its defense and its shooting. The Suns beat a short-handed Magic team without Paolo Banchero, Jalen Suggs and Jonathan Isaac, 117-104, to improve to 2-5. Phoenix was short Mark Williams, Jordan Goodwin, and Rasheer Fleming.

Orlando outrebounded Phoenix by 15 and got to the line 11 more times, but the Magic turned it over 25 times, and the Suns hit 17 threes. A 23-point lead after three quarters was more than enough to survive a late Orlando push.

Devin Booker: 30 points (11-of-22 FG, 4-of-8 3PT, 4-of-4 FT), 8 assists, 3 steals, +16 in 34 minutes

Dillon Brooks: 24 points (9-of-16 FG, 4-of-6 3PT), 2 steals, +12 in 29 minutes

Miles Bridges: 18 points (6-of-10 FG, 3-of-6 3PT), 13 rebounds, 5 assists, +12 in 31 minutes

Orlando came out firing. The Magic got whatever they wanted early and jumped out to a 14-8 lead.

Then the Suns started taking the ball away. Orlando turned it over nine times in the quarter, and Phoenix turned those mistakes into 13 points, mostly in transition. Anthony Black had four of those giveaways by himself.

Devin Booker played all 12 minutes and set the tone with 12 points, hitting a pair of threes and going perfect at the line. The Suns hit five threes as a team to Orlando's three, which covered for getting outworked on the glass and in the paint.

The bench changed the game. Ryan Dunn, Collin Gillespie and Man Man all finished the quarter on the plus side, and Phoenix pushed the lead to nine before Orlando got the last bucket to cut it to seven entering Q2.

Phoenix led after the first quarter, 33-26.

Luke Kennard owned the second quarter. He came off the bench and went 3-for-3 from deep for 12 points, giving Phoenix a second scorer while Orlando keyed in on Booker.

Booker kept cooking anyway. He added 11 more in the quarter on efficient shooting and went into the locker room with 23.

Orlando stayed close by crashing the glass and living at the line. The Magic grabbed nine offensive rebounds in the quarter and got to the stripe 14 times, but they missed six of those free throws and couldn't buy a three. Wendell Carter Jr. did most of the damage inside with 10 in the quarter.

Man Man didn't score, but he was a team-best +13 in his minutes.

The three-point line is the story. Phoenix hit 10 threes in the half and Orlando hit four. The Magic shot better inside and controlled the boards, but the Suns' shooting and Orlando's turnovers built the cushion.

Booker leads all scorers with 23 points on 8-of-13 shooting, including 3-of-4 from three and 4-of-4 at the line. Kennard has 12 off the bench.

Dillon Brooks took over the third. He scored 12 in the quarter on 5-of-7 shooting, and Miles Bridges added 10 more as the starters blew the game open.

Orlando's turnover problem came back in a big way. The Magic gave it away 10 times in the quarter, and Phoenix's defense jumped passing lanes all period with six steals.

Booker only scored three in the quarter, but he didn't need to. He set up teammates with four assists, and every Suns starter finished the period at +7 or better. Man Man chipped in a pair of buckets off the bench.

After three, Phoenix led 96-73. The Suns outscored Orlando 33-22 in the third quarter.

Orlando kept its starters on the floor and made a push, winning the quarter by 10. Carter didn't miss in the fourth, going 4-for-4, and the Magic knocked down five threes in the period.

Phoenix rested Booker and most of the starting group for long stretches, and the offense cooled off with five turnovers and three missed free throws in the quarter.

The deep bench closed it out, with Koa Peat, Jamaree Bouyea, Duop Reath and Pat Spencer getting the final minutes. Phoenix won 117-104.

Kevin Durant returns to the Valley on Saturday night as the Suns host the Houston Rockets.
