#2853. #PostPulpit mailbag: Will the Patriots be buyers or sellers at the trade deadline?

It's a busy weekend in Foxboro as Rob Gronkowski and the 2016 Patriots are back in town, while the current New England Patriots squad has a big game themselves against the Green Bay Packers days before the trade deadline.

Before all the action begins, let's get into this week's edition of the #PostPulpit Mailbag.

Trade talk! Would they really trade Barmore? I could see it if they were 3-5, but seems like it would leave them very weak at a position that isn't terribly strong to begin with in a year when everything is still on the table in front of you. Maybe that's a move you make in the offseason, no? – RRDMuz

My belief entering this year was that this is Christian Barmore's last season in New England. Barmore has no guaranteed money remaining on his contract and the value of the deal has not matched his play since his return from blood clots. Pair that with long-term concerns over a lingering knee injury and it would make sense to move on.

As for the rest of this season, however, I'd still expect him and Carlton Davis to be on the roster at this time next week.

Where's the line between buy and sell? How do you think they see this beat-up team's chances for a deep playoff run? Moving Barmore weakens them badly for this year, so maybe if that's happening it's not worth adding pieces? If it doesn't, maybe some depth? Or do they just stay the course and any playoff appearance or win becomes gravy? – ed.liebfried

With Drake Maye and Mike Vrabel, the Patriots will always have a chance to compete and make a run in the playoffs. When it comes to selling, I do think there's a logical argument for getting younger and adding draft capital, but the time and place for that is next offseason.

At this deadline, I think the Patriots will focus on finding minor upgrades to bolster the roster. The best-case scenario would be finding the next version of Kyle Van Noy, who they acquired in exchange for a late-round pick swap.

And while I hate when teams like the Red Sox use injured players returning as a reason not to be active at the deadline, I think it's a different story in football. The Patriots getting players back like Mack Hollins, Romeo Doubs and Alijah Vera-Tucker in upcoming weeks are a significant boost to the roster.

What's up with Henderson and the trade talk? Not a culture fit? Or system fit?? It seems odd he's not even practicing – Groganator

Henderson has now missed over a week with a legitimate illness, which is why he has been absent. The trade speculation stems from some of his struggles this season, but I wouldn't be ready to give up on the 24-year-old second-round pick, who posted over 1,100 yards and 10 touchdowns last season.

The hope should be that Henderson can get healthy from both his illness and ankle injury and that the coaching staff can find a way to get him going on the field.

If this team is fully healthy where would you look to improve – XGhost-PepperX

As we discussed, we are expecting more minor additions to the roster. With wide receivers and linemen coming back from injury, a blocking tight end would be the main spot we'd look on offense. Part of the run game issues have been with the tight ends blocking the edges as that is not Hunter Henry's game and Eli Raridon has had up-and-down moments like most rookies.

On defense, the defensive line has played better in recent weeks but a true nose tackle and edge rusher — as they still only three on the roster — would be players to add. Another linebacker to allow the defense to play more true base defense against heavier personnel groupings could also be a target.

Williams, Douglas, and Chism were productive against Miami. Was that because it was Miami? Or, in the playoffs, might we have 6-8 skill position players who are dangerous? – WannaBe Pats GM

We've been in the camp that all three are quality wide receivers in this league. They might not be bonafide No. 1 options, but they all have unique skillsets that make that strong complimentary pieces who can also take on larger roles when players above them are injured.

We'll also continue to push for more Kyle Williams snaps, specifically in the slot like he was used in college. He's a dangerous player with his speed and the Patriots should look to exploit that more.

Will the New England Patriots activate both WR Mack Hollins and FB Reggie Gilliam this week? – For Pats Sake

Hollins looks ready to go. Gilliam isn't ready yet but has increased his presence in the locker room in the past week.

With so many QB injuries around the league, do you think one of our QBs have some value to bring good draft value (not a sixth round) or some one we can exchange with? – sumeetw

Tommy DeVito has started games in the league so could have some attraction. But, I'd say the injuries around the league show how valuable it is to have depth at that position. Any quality backup quarterback is more valuable for a competing team compared to a late-round draft pick.

That's all for this week's #PostPulpit mailbag. If you have questions you'd liked to be answered next week, submit them online in our weekly submission post on the Feed. Make sure to follow @iambrianhines and @PatsPulpit as well.

#2851. Preview: Utah Jazz head for a rodeo in Dallas

The sky is falling. The Utah Jazz remain winless thus far in November, on the cusp of a six-game losing streak. The team is shooting 27.6% on wide-open threes and has been trailing the bottom of nearly every statistical category. But just maybe, just maybe, all they need is a good ol' NBA Cup Tournament match to light a competitive spirit under them.

That's right, the Dallas Mavericks host the Utah Jazz at the American Airlines Center for an Emirates NBA Cup West Group A showdown. Dallas has already gained an early 1-0 advantage in the Cup standings in their 116-111 victory over the Rockets just last week. The NBA Cup has not been favorable towards the Jazz since its inauguration; in fact, it's given teams more of an excuse to continue brutally beating up tanking teams — point differential matters!

Over the past few years, the Jazz have held records of:

But now that they're playing for wins (or so we've been told), we could see the script flipped. After all, it's a 'blank slate' for this young team. They've battled through injuries, have been a part of two overtime games, and have been through some of the worst shooting woes in years. But that's only temporary, right?

Dallas has likely been content with the Cooper Flagg-Kyrie Irving pairing, given that their team is 4-4 and has lost to some of the league's best. The Mavs play an incredibly fast brand of basketball, ranking among the league leaders in overall pace and fast-break points.

Obviously, Utah won't be able to put the reigning Rookie of the Year to a complete stop, but this team has to make an effort to command their presence in the paint. The Jazz allowed an unanswered 12-0 run by New Orleans in overtime just 48 hours ago, exclusively inside the arc. We saw them hold Zion Williamson completely scoreless in the first half, but all hell broke loose after they surrendered a 13-point lead. We'll have to hope that they can put out the same energy as they did against a conference foe like Flagg.

You could consider Cooper Flagg as an honorary 'Jazz Killer'. In his two career matchups, he averages 34.0 points, 8.5 rebounds and 7.0 assists. Though, the Jazz have won both of those matches. Now, with a reinforced Mavs squad around him, Utah can't roll into Dallas with a smug grin.

The numbers don't lie; Flagg has struggled tremendously from deep early into the season, shooting 7-of-33 from outside this season. Utah will have to force Flagg into uncomfortable shots that take him away from the line, where he converts 55.9% of his two-point attempts.

Because of his promoted role as a secondary playmaker, they should also employ a player like Ace or Okogie to pressure him into his loose handle and perhaps cough up a few turnovers — Flagg is averaging 3.1 turnovers per game in the early going of the season.

As one of the rising superstars in the West, he's transcended a typical 'sophomore slump' to turn Dallas into a legitimate playoff team this year. Finding a way to slow down this multifaceted star will be a burden on this team for the foreseeable future.

This has been a popular piece circulating Jazz Twitter:

Through the first eight games, the furthest milestone Peterson has achieved is really only being thrust in the starting lineup. He's averaged an honest 30.3 minutes per game, but the question is, why hasn't it felt like it?

He shares the ball with a dominant guard like Keyonte George, who completely dictates the tempo of the offense. Peterson's role shifts to that of a more complementary piece — a player that the team can chuck the ball to throw up a Hail Mary before the shot clock expires. Coach Hardy runs an egalitarian, pass-and-cut offensive system where Peterson is used to distort the defense rather than being a centerpiece.

Of course, he has his rookie mistakes too: he's hitting just 35.4% of his field-goal attempts, struggling to find a consistent rhythm inside the arc, particularly on his floater attempts. That could look particularly concerning, considering that he was noted for his lack of vertical burst coming out of the draft.

But after looking at the Darius Acuff Jr. template over at Sacramento (not recommended if you want to win basketball games), the coaching staff needs to realize they have DARRYN PETERSON on their squad. This is to hope they could have more plays run for him: perhaps using him more as a post-up guard, or having him be the one to leak up the court in transition.

If the Jazz are going to be without Jackson Jr. for a couple of months at least, and if Lauri Markkanen is unable to break out of his shooting slump, Peterson will need to play an integral part of the offensive flow moving forward.

Speaking of Lauri, the most unprecedented story coming out of this 1-7 start has been the Finnish Star's efficiency. Of course, we all saw him injure his wrist in the showdown against the Grizzlies, which has had lingering issues due to the dependence on his wrist snap & flick, but this is going to be an integral year for Lauri.

The drop-off has been stark: he's averaging 17.1 points per game — down significantly since his career peak and is converting just 38.7% of his field-goal attempts. The Hardy revolution has completely eradicated Markkanen's inside-the-arc scoring, having him attempt a wild 8.3 three-point attempts a game.

He's also been forced to occasionally shift as a small-ball center due to the banged-up injuries of Jackson Jr. and Nurkic, which was noticeably felt when the Pelicans destroyed the Jazz in the paint during the OT period.

"I think he's playing through a lot of pain right now. I think he's really battling for his teammates and us", Will Hardy said about Lauri Markkanen on Wednesday.

Of course, Markkanen will not have as wild a slump as he does for the rest of the season. He'll regain his efficiency. His wrist will eventually heal. Really, it's just a tough spot to be in when your team's record is 1-7.

#2850. As Chargers' offense struggles, Mike McDaniel will move from the sideline to the booth

Chargers offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel will get a different perspective on his struggling offense on Sunday against the Texans.

McDaniel said today that he will move upstairs to the booth to call plays after previously working from the sideline.

“One of the things that I want to try is call plays from the box to see adjustments for myself and communicate with the position coaches appropriately what things we can focus on between series,” McDaniel said. “I won’t be in the same spot.”

Although the Chargers’ offense has been among the worst in the NFL this season and head coach Jim Harbaugh has faced questions about whether he should fire his offensive coordinator, McDaniel insisted that he’s not concerned about the criticism.

“My problem solving doesn’t come from insecurity,” McDaniel said. “I’m not trying to prove or justify anything.”

The Chargers rank dead last in the NFL in scoring, having scored only 99 points this season, and they have an NFL-high 17 turnovers. McDaniel said he thinks it’s worth trying something different while delegating some of what he had been doing on the sideline to the assistant coaches.

“Seems like a good action to take based on how things have gone this year, and realistically something that I’ve only brought up because I’ve observed, I’m very confident in the rest of the offensive coaching staff and how they’re able to set the tone and communicate information on the sidelines. So I feel a little more comfortable to try that,” McDaniel said.

If that doesn’t work, Harbaugh’s next step might be to move McDaniel from the booth to the unemployment line.

#2848. NFL predictions: 4 keys to a Lions victory over the Dolphins

The Detroit Lions (5-2) and Miami Dolphins (1-6) will face off in Week 9 in a battle between two teams at different stages in their regime builds. The Lions have their eyes firmly set on the postseason and are riding a three-game win streak, while the Dolphins are in the early stages of a rebuild and are performing much like the Lions did in 2021 and 2022—lots of grit, but struggling to find success.

"(Dolphins Head) Coach (Jeff) Hafley's done a good job in his first year," Lions coach Dan Campbell said on Wednesday. "A lot of similarities to—just reminds me a little of what we were when we came in. They're young, they're hungry, they're active. They run, they hit, they hustle, they finish, try to play disciplined ball, and they're playing that way."

This week's prediction preview is sponsored by the folks at FanDuel Sportsbook, who currently have the Lions listed at +1600 to win this year's Super Bowl and are currently 7-point favorites in Week 9. Let's take a closer look at this matchup and predict how the Lions will earn a victory over the Dolphins in this week's Honolulu Blueprint.

For a detailed look at the opposing scheme, check out our complementary breakdown piece: Lions Week 9 preview: Breaking down the Dolphins' offensive and defensive schemes.

Last Sunday, the Lions faced arguably the best defense in the NFL when they went head-to-head with the Vikings, and while the Dolphins are on the opposite end of the rankings spectrum, some of the strategies the Lions used against Minnesota will transfer over to this week's game against Miami.

The Dolphins defense enters this game 29th in DVOA, 24th in points allowed (25.9), 24th in yards allowed per play (5.7 ypp), and are dead last in the NFL in three areas: EPA per play (+0.10), EPA per pass allowed (+0.26), and passing yards allowed per play (8.3).

However, this defense is showing growth in pressure rate. Looking at season totals, the Dolphins' pressure numbers could be a bit deceiving: 31st in total pressures (77), 18th in pressure rate (35.6%), 30th in total sacks (9), and 28th in sack rate (4.2%). But when you look at the splits from their last four games, you can see the improvement:

at Vikings: 17 pressures, 39.5% pressure rate, 4 sacks, 9.3% sack rate

vs. Bengals: 11 pressures, 33.3% pressure rate, 0 sacks, 0% sack rate

at Jets: 15 pressures, 45.5% pressure rate, 2 sacks, 6.1% sack rate

vs. Patriots: 13 pressures, 48.1% pressure rate, 3 sacks, 11.1% sack rate

If we isolate the games against the Vikings, Jets, and Patriots, we see nearly 60% of the defensive pressures and 100% of the Dolphins sacks. When you look at how the Dolphins have generated pressures and sacks, most of those situations come from stunting their defensive linemen. Last week against the Patriots, the Dolphins sacked the quarterback once on an end-of-half situation, with the other two sacks coming off a stunt where an edge rusher loops behind the interior defensive lineman and twists inside. We also saw stunts get home against the Vikings in Week 4.

To counter the Dolphins' stunts, offenses have been attacking the middle of the defensive line with their rushing attacks; teams are running inside 53% of the time, the sixth-highest rate in the NFL.

While the Lions have preferred to lean on their outside-zone rushing scheme, we saw last week against the Vikings that Detroit has a formula to get downhill on inside runs. Now, the Lions don't necessarily need to deploy a full-house set (three players in the backfield) again, but it would certainly be effective against the Dolphins' Wide-9 base 4-3 defense.

While all defenses are complex, at their core, the Dolphins split their defensive personnel almost evenly between a base 4-3 (three linebackers) front and a "Big Nickel" (three safeties) formation. Regardless of set, they spend about 80% of the time in zone coverage, with half of that time spent between single-high (Cover-1, -3) and two-high (Cover-2, -4, -6) safety sets. When they deploy man coverage, they run exclusively single-high Cover-1.

Depending on the safety formation, Lions quarterback Jared Goff will have to find the holes in the zone to exploit, but those gaps can widen if the Lions stretch the Dolphins laterally with their passing game. Based on the games I watched, the Dolphins' defenders settle in their zones and tend to be slow to react to crossing routes in front of them. When offenses find success on crossers and stretch the zones across the field, that opens gaps down the deep seams, where speed receivers—hey, Jameson Williams—have found chunk plays.

If the Lions can slow the Dolphins' pass rush with run up the middle, then stretch the secondary laterally, they'll have an opportunity to chew up yards in a variety of ways.

When the Dolphins lost their dynamic running back De'Von Achane to an ACL injury in Week 3, many thought Miami's rushing attack would struggle. However, second-year back Ollie Gordon has stepped into a starting role, and the Dolphins' new downhill, physical rushing attack has proved to be an asset, even outproducing their early-season statistics, save last week vs. the Patriots. With quarterback Malik Willis adding another element to the run game through RPOs and scrambles, stopping the run will likely be the Lions' top priority.

On paper, their raw numbers look good: rushing for 123.3 yards per game (11th), averaging 4.4 yards per carry (11th), -0.03 EPA per rush (10th), 26 runs that gain 10+ yards (7th), and explosive runs 16.7% (3rd).

However, there are some concerning numbers that point to struggles with consistency, including:

The Dolphins will want to establish their rushing attack against the Lions, and Detroit will need to match that downhill physicality. It wouldn't be surprising to see the Lions spend a lot of time in base early as both teams work to control the trenches. Expect seven and eight defenders in the box pre-snap, and a situational spy to track Willis is likely.

With changes coming to the Lions' linebacker roles, Detroit will need Derrick Barnes, Trevor Nowaske, and Malcolm Rodriguez to elevate their games and keep the explosive runs in check.

If the Dolphins can establish the run, they do a nice job of running play-action behind it and finding success. But that's not always an option for Miami's offense, and the inconsistencies in the run game have forced Willis to create opportunities on his own.

Willis is talented—we saw that in Green Bay—comfortable passing from the pocket, and able to extend plays by escaping outside. But with limited support, he holds onto the ball too long, takes sacks, or misses his targets because his accuracy gets loose/inconsistent on the run. Miami's offensive line is average at best (see below) and doesn't hold up well against pressure, and while the Dolphins receivers have unique skills, they lack a true playmaker and currently rely on two rookies—Caleb Douglas and Chris Bell—in starting wide receiver roles.

As a result, Miami's passing offense numbers are near the bottom of the league:

The Lions would benefit by giving Willis no relief. Entering this game, the Lions have registered 116 pressures (5th best), a 35.8% pressure rate (17th), 24 sacks (third most), and a 7.4% sack rate (7th). Defense has found success against the Dolphins by rushing four and sending the blitz, so the Lions should have options to create pressure; they just need to find the right elixir to disrupt Willis.

#2847. John Lynch on Brandon Aiyuk: We'll look for a path that works for both sides

Brandon Aiyuk filed for reinstatement from the 49ers’ left squad list this week and he’s expected to be at the team’s facility on Friday to take the next step in resuming his football career.

Once he is reinstated, the 49ers will have a choice between keeping him on the active roster, trading him or releasing him. The latter option is seen as the likeliest given the lack of trade interest earlier this year and both head coach Kyle Shanahan and General Manager John Lynch saying that Aiyuk is done playing for the Niners.

Shanahan said on Wednesday that his thinking hasn’t changed and Lynch said on KNBR Thursday that the team is working with the league to come up with the best solution.

“Look, I think the way I’ll characterize it, number one, we’ve got a 6-1 football team that we think has really got a shot at this thing this year,” Lynch said. “So our focus is going to remain on this team. Kyle spoke of that yesterday. Having said that, I have a job to do, and it entails a lot of different things. This is kind of a unique situation, not one you have — so there’s really no playbook, but I always go back to what’s my charge, what’s my job. My job is to look out for the best interests of the 49ers, and as such, in this particular situation, we’re working with the NFL management council to navigate through kind of a different situation. It’s fluid. I’m going to kinda leave it at that because I’ve been recommended to do so, and I think it’s the right thing to do. We’ll look for a pathway for both sides here that works. Next week we can talk a little more in detail about the process because kind of a fluid situation.”

Lynch said generally that anything is possible when asked if there’s any way Aiyuk could return to the team and said the wideout’s new agent Drew Rosenhaus “is a good guy to deal with” before reiterating that he’d have more to say in the future about the entire situation.

#2846. What makes this 76ers team stacked with superstars so unique

What makes this 76ers team stacked with superstars so unique originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

They're a team of superstars that don't play superstar basketball.

That's the beauty of this 76ers team. They play a brand of unselfish team-first basketball you rarely see from a team loaded with stars.

LeBron James is one of the two or three greatest players in NBA history, a four-time MVP, a four-time NBA champion, a 1st-ballot Hall of Famer.

Joel Embiid is a seven-time all-star, a former MVP, an Olympic gold medalist and a likely Hall of Famer.

Jaylen Brown is a five-time all-star, an NBA champion, a career 20 points-per-game scorer.

Tyrese Maxey is a two-time all-star, one of only two NBA guards averaging 27.0 points per game over the last four years.

Four certified megastars on one team. And somehow they've figured out how to leave their egos at the front door and play smart, tough, disciplined team basketball, the style of ball you just never see on these superstar-laden teams.

On offense, they patiently work the ball around, always looking for the open man or a positive matchup. You've got this bunch of big-name, high-priced All-Stars who are just as happy to pass the ball as shoot it. That never happens.

The 76ers are sixth in the NBA in assists, and they're one of only four teams with twice as many assists as turnovers. Smart, unselfish, patient, disciplined.

When an all-timer like LeBron averages 7.3 assists per game that speaks volumes. LeBron is fifth in the NBA in assists per game among forwards, which is wild. You can see the joy on his face when one of his passes leads to a basket. When one of the greatest players in history has that mentality, it rubs off on everyone around him.

Embiid hasn't really got going yet on offense and still takes too many 3's, but he's also embraced the team-first mentality, and his 4.8 assists per game are more than one full assist above his career average and 4th-most in the NBA among centers or forward-centers. And still one of the most dominating defensive players in the league.

Brown is averaging 27.0 points, which you expect, but he's also averaging 4.3 assists per game, significantly above his career average of 3.8 coming into the season. He's fit in so well so fast you forget its his first season here.

And what can you even say about Maxey? Just a beast. He's averaging nearly 30 points per game but never wastes a possession, always makes the right decision with the ball in his hands and is still finding time to average 4.3 assists per game.

With James, Embiid, Brown and Maxey, the 76ers are the only NBA team with four guys averaging at least 16 points and 4 assists per game. Only the Pacers, Magic and Raptors have three.

But where we're really seeing this group playing out of their minds is on the defensive end, where this bunch of all-stars, including two newcomers, has been astounding.

The 76ers have the 2nd-best defensive efficiency rating in the league, behind only the Pistons, who they play Wednesday night, and they're allowing the 2nd-fewest points in the league, also behind Detroit. Last year, they allowed 123 points per game through eight games. This year they're at 111.

They're holding teams to 43 percent shooting from the field, 3rd-best in the league and their lowest since 2011-12. Their 9.3 steals per game are 6th-most.

All five starters are among the top 25 players in the league in defensive rating – James is fourth, Embiid 11th, Edgecombe 15th, Maxey 22nd and Brown 23rd. How is that even possible?

It's rare to see superstar-caliber guys play as hard on the defensive end as the offensive end. Everybody on this team embraces it. They hustle, they work, they communicate and most importantly they commit to it.

The biggest concern when the 76ers built this dream team was that it would be a team of individuals out for themselves, but the reality has been the opposite.

In a very short period of time, they've learned how to play together. How to play for each other.

And we haven't even mentioned V.J. Edgecomb, who at 21 years old has figured out how to assimilate into this loaded lineup, never force anything, wait for his opportunities and make huge shots when he gets his turn. Edgecombe is at 12.7 points and 3.0 assists per game, and his numbers are understandably down a bit from last year, but if that bothers him it sure doesn't show.

And the role players – Dean Wade, Anfernee Simons, Kentavious Caldwell-Pope, Jabari Walker – have each adopted the same ego-free style of basketball, supporting the starters however they need to.

Nick Nurse deserves a ton of credit for getting this bunch to play this brand of hoops. It's not easy to get any NBA player to put team goals ahead of individual goals. But he's got Hall of Famers and all-stars doing it and having a blast along the way. They all seem to love playing basketball the right way and they seem to love playing together.

The 76ers are 7-1 and looking like a real threat to win the East, and they're doing it by playing the game the right way.

By committing to each other and not themselves.

#2844. The July 2026 Red Sox were never out of the game… even when fans were

Before we begin looking ahead to 2027, OTM is looking back at 2026, highlighting some of the biggest, strangest, and most memorable moments of a memorable season. Today, we look at an unlikely comeback in the middle of the streak.

A few days ago, before the Ravens-Bills matchup, ESPN ran a parody ad on folks who left a 2025 game early, as Josh Allen and the Bills found themselves down two possessions in the fourth quarter. The Bills, to the ire of this Patriots fan, would win that primetime game last year, and Josh Allen, never one to mince words in his postgame interviews, said "Our team didn't quit. I mean, I think there's people that left the stadium. That's OK. We'll be fine. But have some faith next time." The camera then cut to some folks who were in the parking lot during Allen's comeback, and I found myself laughing at Buffalo fans, as is often easy to do amongst their deep playoff runs filled with hope, their chirps that at least Allen would win an MVP, and celebrations of October records. Of course they'd leave this game early, and how funny it was that they weren't able to see how brilliant their quarterback was in the clutch in person!

I then recoiled in horror as I realized that, just four months ago, on one fateful afternoon much further downstate in Flushing, I did the exact same thing to our beloved Red Sox.

In my first year of being a resident of the Capital Region, New York, it has been easier for me to hit the Big Apple than Boston. I circled the Mets-Red Sox series in my calendar for the middle of July, reluctantly, as the Red Sox did not start the season very well and the game would be directly before the All-Star game. By the day of the game, though, I was very bullish on this Red Sox team. The Red Sox were winners of eight consecutive games, and it didn't much matter if those wins came against the Angels and the White Sox, the latter of whom, at the time, weren't the formidable contender they ended up becoming later in the season, but were certainly no slouches. The team had awakened offensively against the Angels and was showing definite signs of life

This was not the case, though, in the early innings of this game against the Mets, after my trip down 87. The Red Sox had trouble getting anything going against a lanky lefty Zac Thornton. Thornton ended up being a bright spot in an otherwise hapless season for the Mets, but he was on the mound for the first time in what was already his third call-up of the season from Triple-A Syracuse. His first try resulted in the Nationals taking him for five runs in 4 1/3 innings. It was fine for the offensive to flounder while I was watching – I had seen it plenty of times this season. But did the bats have to flounder so harshly while the wonderful Obsession star Inde Navarette was in attendance? No, no, no, no, no, don't do that! I thought we were having a nice win streak!

If matters weren't bad enough, this was a scheduled short appearance from Payton Tolle, who looked serviceable for a bit longer, striking out Juan Soto with authority (you can watch that clip below) and Brayan Bello, the guy who departed the Major League roster about a month prior to fall in love with baseball again, was up in relief. Frankly, I was writing this game up as a loss mentally, as the Mets lineup did not look punchless so far and Tolle was lucky to have just Francisco Lindor's RBI double after 3 2/3 innings.

But Bello coasted for quite a while. Lindor would be pesky yet again with a home run to make the game 2-0, but that was one of two batters Bello did not retire, and the other one would be victim to a double play, anyway. Bello would pitch through the eighth. The problem, though, is that Thornton was dealing. Through seven, he had given up just two hits, was pitching a shutout, and had struck out five. But, good things can't last forever, and so interim manager Andy Green went to Luke Weaver to start the eighth. At that point, with how hollow the Red Sox's hitting attempts had become, the Red Sox's expected winning percentage was hovering around 7 percent. The Red Sox would go 1-2-3 in the top of the eighth. More of the same.

Enter Devin Williams, and enter my walk to the exit when, after a Ceddanne Rafaela single, he'd unceremoniously retire Abreu with a pop fly. The team's pop was completely nonexistent; why would I subject myself to sitting in more NYC traffic after a loss? It was a sure thing, right? No sooner did my feet hit the closing gate than I heard a roar from a rather divided crowd. Francisco Lindor, the guy who was singlehandedly responsible for the lead the Mets had built, had bobbled the most routine of grounders that would have ended the game. The Red Sox now had men on first and second, and I was left to turn the stream on in the car.

The rest is history as we know it: Devin Williams would walk in the Red Sox's first run of the game. Aroldis Chapman would start warming, Jarren Duran would have a clutch RBI knock, the game would go to the bottom of the 9th inning all tied up at 2, Chapman would be every bit of the historically dependable reliever we've come to know to send the game to extras, the top of the tenth would see the Red Sox playing small ball extremely efficiently, scoring the Manfred runner Masataka Yoshida on two consecutive plays. The small ball was a welcome addition to their game plan, and on that Sunday, it was due to their trust in the man who'd come in to close the game out, Garrett Whitlock, who slammed the door the same way I slammed my door when I arrived to it in the parking lot.

The Red Sox were winners of nine consecutive games going into the All-Star break, a streak that would last two more series. Even better, they were in that situation thanks to contributions — 13 outs in relief, to be exact — from a guy who was one of the reasons the season starting so dire in the first place. On July 12, Bello was electric, and so began a summer that made it exciting to root for Brayan Bello's growth and success again. They were finding ways to win. I guess, as Josh Allen put it so eloquently, when dealing with a team I should be confident in, I'll have more faith next time.

#2840. Joe Milton on his first start: The NFL is about being ready when your number is called

Joe Milton has never started an NFL game. The closest he came was in Week 18 of the 2024 season when Patriots starter Drake Maye played only three snaps before giving way to Milton, who played the final 61 snaps.

Milton looked like a starting NFL quarterback in that game, completing 22 of 29 passes for 241 yards and a touchdown.

Less than two years later, Milton is on his third team and has played only 51 snaps in four appearances with Dallas since.

He will make his first career start on Sunday when the Eagles play the Giants.

“I was just pretty much going through the plays, going through the week like I was a starter, or like I was playing, and just being ready,” Milton said Thursday, via Olivia Reiner of the Philadelphia Inquirer. “And that’s what the NFL is about: Just being ready when your name is called, and just preparing for those moments.”

The Eagles signed Milton off the Cowboys’ practice squad on Oct. 16 after they placed Jalen Hurts on injured reserve due to blood clots. Tanner McKee started the past three games, but went 0-3 as the Eagles ran their losing streak to six games.

Milton has had a crash course in learning the playbook and the terminology, which he said reminds him of the West Coast scheme he had in New England his rookie season.

Milton was asked how much of the Eagles’ playbook he knows.

“Shoot, whatever’s in this week,” he said with a laugh.

#2839. Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double

Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers stayed unbeaten Saturday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena, earning a 127-116 win over the Bucks and improving to 3-0 on the season.

Joel Embiid had his 10th career regular-season triple-double, tallying 28 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists.

On his 30th birthday, Jaylen Brown posted 27 points and five assists. Tyrese Maxey had 26 points. VJ Edgecombe scored 17 and grabbed 13 boards.

The Sixers' absences on the first night of a back-to-back included LeBron James (low back/sciatica management). Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said pregame that he did not know yet who would be available for his team's matchup with the Pistons on Sunday.

Here are observations on the Sixers' victory Saturday:

Dean Wade made his Sixers debut and started in James' place. He'd missed the first two games of the regular season with a left ankle sprain.

The 3-and-D forward scored the night's first points by a sinking a corner three-pointer on the opening possession.

Embiid also had a sharp start. He moved well, made good decisions and served as the main hub of his team's offense in the early going.

The Sixers' seven-time All-Star center has often enjoyed facing Myles Turner. He entered the night with an average of 29.4 points in 18 previous games against the Bucks big man.

Embiid did a little bit of everything in the first quarter, posting eight points, four assists and four rebounds over nine minutes. After snatching an offensive board, Embiid drained a fadeaway jumper to give the Sixers a 10-1 lead.

One of Embiid's assists was quite stylish. He found Edgecombe open beyond the arc with a behind-the-back bounce pass. Edgecombe knocked down the shot and wound up going 3 for 4 from three-point range in the first quarter.

The Sixers added rookie Labaron Philon Jr. to their rotation. Jabari Walker stayed in the mix, though he didn't enter until the 7:36 mark of the second quarter.

Philon played four minutes in his NBA debut and missed his lone shot attempt, a corner three. On defense, Philon allowed a couple of blow-bys off the dribble. He generally looked like he belonged on offense, albeit without any production in his brief run.

Maxey banked in a half-court heave at the first-quarter buzzer to put the Sixers up nine points. The Sixers couldn't carry forward any momentum, however, and began the second quarter poorly.

Adem Bona had another rough stint amid a subpar start to the season. After Anfernee Simons missed a transition layup try, Ryan Rollins' three lifted the Bucks into a 40-37 lead.

The dreadful stretch for the Sixers on both sides of the ball called to mind how they'd fallen into a 29-point deficit Thursday night vs. the Cavaliers before clawing out a comeback win.

The Sixers mustered just seven points in first six minutes of the second quarter and had many stagnant possessions that concluded with contested jumpers. The team's transition defense was dismal for much of the second period. Milwaukee had the game's first 19 fast-break points.

The Sixers regained the lead late in the second quarter. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope made two three-balls in the second and nabbed three first-half steals. Embiid assisted a go-ahead, and-one Walker layup.

Brown hit a three with 11.8 seconds left in the second quarter. Unsurprisingly, his variety of shotmaking skills were useful without James in the lineup.

Even when James or Embiid sit, the Sixers should have a simple advantage in terms of volume of stars over most opponents this year. None of Brown, Embiid or Maxey had the sort of off night that would have improved the Bucks' odds of a road win. They'd all passed the 20-point mark by the end of the third quarter.

Maxey notched another final-possession bucket, this time with a more conventional make. He canned a jumper from the right elbow with 1.7 seconds left in the third to extend the Sixers' lead to 97-87.

The Bucks made a late push in the fourth quarter. Kel'el Ware's put-back, and-one layup cut the Milwaukee's deficit to 117-114.

The Sixers ultimately handled business. Embiid reached his triple-double by assisting a second-chance Brown jumper and and Caldwell-Pope soon drilled a dagger corner three. Embiid even threw down a last-minute dunk for good measure.

For the second consecutive season, the Sixers have a 3-0 start. They got to four wins last year before dropping their first game.

The National League North side welcome the former Premier League and FA Cup winners to The MGroup Stadium in the first round of this season's competition, under the lights on their artificial pitch.

From playing against Messi and Ronaldo to non-league

Forestieri ready for fresh challenge at Oxford City

Oxford City have made it to the first round proper for the first time in four years, having narrowly beaten Torquay United in the final qualifying round.

Pollock, 25, has personal experience of an Oxford City shock.

And he believes the pressure is all on the third-tier Foxes, who have struggled in their start to the League One campaign following back-to-back relegations from the Premier League and the Championship.

"There's just a feeling of excitement among us really," Pollock added.

"The pressure's on them to do well in the league and in the cup - we're at home and we know the pitch so it favours us in that aspect.

"That being said, we know they're a good team so we have to be up for it. Oxford City have done cup upsets before and there is no reason why we can't do it again."

Pollock has had a somewhat unique footballing journey, first making a name for himself on YouTube with Hashtag United.

Spencer Owen co-founded Hashtag with his brother Seb Carmichael-Brown in 2016 and ran an academy series on their channel in 2017.

Pollock ended up winning the series and then played for their first team, starring in a charity game called the Wembley Cup where he won man of the match and was rewarded with a trial at Premier League side Crystal Palace.

A year later he moved to Northampton, where he made 29 senior appearances, scoring two goals.

"They were trying to find the next star," he recalled of the Hashtag series, having applied for it when he was just 16.

"I didn't think anything of it when I applied for it and I ended up winning it out of 20,000 people.

"It was a good experience when I was younger and I got to play men's football from a young age so it's helped a lot in my career."

Sixers-Cavs by the numbers: Pressure, threes and a 29-point rematch originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers and Cavaliers have already played one game that looked like two.

Cleveland led by 29 points during the Sixers' home opener on Oct. 22 and carried a 69-45 advantage into halftime. Philadelphia responded by winning the second half, 69-37, and completing a 114-106 comeback.

It was the Sixers' largest comeback since the NBA began maintaining detailed play-by-play data in 1997-98. Only nine other teams during that span had overcome a deficit of at least 29 points.

Fifteen days later, the teams will meet again Friday night at Rocket Arena. This time, the matchup counts toward the NBA Cup standings.

The 8-1 Sixers have won five consecutive games and opened group play with a 98-93 victory over the Knicks. The 4-4 Cavs have dropped two straight and will make their Cup debut.

Here are five numbers that help frame the rematch.

Philadelphia's comeback required more than a hot shooting stretch.

The Sixers committed 15 turnovers in the first half, allowing Cleveland to build a 22-6 advantage in points off turnovers. Their pressure then changed the game after halftime.

The Cavs committed 21 turnovers by the end of the night. What had been a 16-point Cleveland advantage in points off turnovers finished even at 22 apiece.

"They upped their pressure and physicality," Cavs head coach Kenny Atkinson said after the game. "It was pretty clear. We did not handle it well."

The Sixers scored 64 of their 69 second-half points through their starting lineup. Tyrese Maxey finished with 28 points, and Philadelphia turned a game that appeared finished into a franchise-record comeback.

The first half of the opening meeting now looks like an exception.

The Sixers have committed 12.9 turnovers per 100 possessions this season, the NBA's second-lowest rate. They are also third in turnover differential, averaging 3.4 fewer giveaways than their opponents.

That is notable for a team that entered the season intending to play faster. Philadelphia has pushed the ball without routinely surrendering possessions.

LeBron James' presence as the primary facilitator has helped. So has Maxey's willingness to move the ball when defenses trap him. Joel Embiid has averaged 5.2 assists, third among qualified centers, and the Sixers have increasingly trusted VJ Edgecombe to make decisions late in games.

Cleveland's defense has not forced many mistakes. The Cavs enter Friday near the bottom of the league in opponent turnover rate.

The first meeting swung when the Sixers stopped giving away possessions and forced Cleveland into mistakes of its own.

The Sixers have allowed 105.1 points per 100 possessions, the NBA's second-best defensive rating. Cleveland enters with the league's ninth-ranked offense.

The Cavs are the only top-10 offense the Sixers have faced through their first nine games.

Philadelphia has held opponents to a 50 percent effective field-goal percentage and 31.8 percent shooting from three-point range. Its defensive shot profile has been encouraging, too. Only 46 percent of opposing three-point attempts have been classified as wide open, the fifth-lowest share in the league, and opponents have taken just 22 percent of their threes from the corners.

There is reason for caution. Based on the quality of shots Philadelphia has allowed, only Washington's opponents have underperformed their expected effective field-goal percentage by a wider margin. The Sixers have defended well, but opponents are unlikely to remain this cold indefinitely.

Cleveland, with Donovan Mitchell, James Harden and Evan Mobley, can test whether those numbers hold against high-level individual shot creation.

The Cavs have attempted exactly 42 three-pointers per game and made 37.2 percent of them.

Cleveland went 7 for 29 from beyond the arc in Philadelphia. Mitchell, Harden and De'Andre Hunter combined to shoot 3 for 17. The Cavs scored 60 points in the paint and still reached 106, but their 24.1 percent performance from three prevented them from stopping the Sixers' comeback.

Friday's game could look considerably different if Cleveland generates its normal volume.

The Sixers have controlled the three-point line well so far, but Mitchell is coming off a 27-point performance against Oklahoma City and scored 32 in the first meeting with Philadelphia. Harden added 16 points that night, although his six turnovers became costly as the Sixers increased their pressure.

Philadelphia has been outrebounded by 5.1 per game. The Cavs rank sixth with 47.5 rebounds per contest.

The Sixers have already shown they can survive a major deficit on the glass. They beat Milwaukee by 11 despite getting outrebounded by 22. That is not a formula they will want to test regularly against Cleveland's size.

Mobley had 18 points and eight rebounds in the first meeting. Jarrett Allen added 14 points and seven boards, helping Cleveland win the rebounding battle, 46-44.

Whether Allen plays Friday remains uncertain.

Cleveland listed Allen as questionable because of a right knee injury after he left Wednesday's loss to Oklahoma City in the first quarter. Allen collided knee-to-knee with Thunder forward Chet Holmgren and did not return.

The Cavs also listed Peyton Watson as questionable with right hamstring soreness and Tyrese Proctor as questionable with an ankle injury. Proctor left Wednesday's game during the fourth quarter. Jaylon Tyson is out with a right ankle sprain.

Allen's availability could significantly alter the matchup on the glass. If he sits, Thomas Bryant would likely handle more of the center minutes behind Mobley. If he plays, Cleveland will have the same starting frontcourt that outrebounded the Sixers during the first meeting.

Atkinson has emphasized the possession battle during Cleveland's two-game slide.

"You've got to get more shots than the other team," he said this week. "Rebounding is a big part of it."

That also carries added importance in the NBA Cup, where point differential is the second tiebreaker after head-to-head results.

Philadelphia enters Friday at 1-0 with a plus-five differential in East Group B. Miami is also 1-0 at plus-20, while Cleveland is playing its first group game.

The Sixers already know they can erase 29 points against the Cavs. A cleaner start would be far more useful than proving it twice.

#2827. Texas high school football powerhouse considers legal action after playoff ban

Argyle Liberty Christian isn't going down without a fight after being kicked out of the TAPPS Division I football playoffs over an eligibility violation.

The Texas high school football powerhouse, considered a favorite to win the state championship, is considering legal action after TAPPS ruled Tuesday, Nov. 3, that the school used an ineligible player and must forfeit games, according to The Dallas Morning News.

"We strongly disagree with the TAPPS ruling and we provided clear and unambiguous evidence to TAPPS which demonstrated our innocence against the false assertions that were made against our football program," the school said in a letter to players' families.

The school called the ruling unfair and said it was exploring legal options to get its team reinstated.

The decision stems from a violation of TAPPS' "follow the coach" rule, which prohibits certain transfer students from competing at the varsity level if they were coached or trained by a coach at their new school within the previous 12 months.

Big wins send Clemens, Canyon Lake into E-N Top 20 football rankings

Multiple sources identified the player as wide receiver Jace Johnson, who transferred from Abilene Cooper before the 2026 season, according to The Dallas Morning News.

TAPPS determined that Johnson previously played on a 7-on-7 team coached by Liberty Christian assistant Antonio Griffin. The organization also said the school's athletic leadership and coaching staff knew or should have known about the connection.

The ruling could also end the high school football career of five-star linebacker Cooper Witten, an Oklahoma commit and son of former Dallas Cowboys star Jason Witten. His father coached Liberty Christian to consecutive TAPPS state championships in 2023 and 2024 before joining Oklahoma's coaching staff.

Cooper's mother, Michelle Witten, disputed the ruling on social media, saying Griffin never coached the player in question and that evidence supporting Liberty Christian was ignored.

TAPPS has revised its eight-team Division I playoff bracket, replacing Liberty Christian with TCA-Addison and delaying the opening round by one week.

Under the revised bracket, San Antonio Central Catholic will face Frisco Legacy Christian in the quarterfinals.

Liberty Christian's postseason hopes now depend on whether the school can successfully challenge the ruling.

#2826. Trevor Lawrence is having by far the best season of his career

Trevor Lawrence has so much talent for the quarterback position that if freshmen could declare for the NFL draft, Lawrence probably would have been the first overall pick in 2019, when he had just led Clemson to a national championship as a true freshman. Instead, Lawrence stayed three years at Clemson and was the first pick in 2021, viewed as a sure-thing quarterback prospect.

In Year 6, Lawrence finally looks like everything he was supposed to be.

Lawrence is having by far the best year of his NFL career, with career-high stats across the board that are constrained only by the fact that the Jaguars win so many blowouts that Lawrence doesn't throw many passes in the fourth quarter.

So far this season, Lawrence has completed 146 of 224 passes for 1,932 yards, with 18 touchdowns, four interceptions and an NFL-leading passer rating of 111.7. Project Lawrence's totals to a 17-game season, and he's on pace to finish with 4,106 yards, 38 touchdowns and nine interceptions. Those are MVP numbers.

Lawrence's rookie year was a disaster, as he led the league in interceptions while playing on a chaotic Jaguars team coached by Urban Meyer, whose only foray into NFL coaching lasted less than one season. Lawrence and the Jaguars got a lot better once they kicked Meyer to the curb, but even in the next three years with Doug Pederson, an offensive coach with a Super Bowl-winning pedigree, Lawrence didn't live up to the pre-draft hype.

Playing in Liam Coen's offense, something has changed. Last year the Jaguars went 13-4, winning double-digit games for the first time since drafting Lawrence, and this year Lawrence and the Jaguars are even better. Lawrence's average of 8.6 yards per pass is the best of his career by almost a yard and a half, a remarkable improvement for any quarterback to make in his sixth season.

Lawrence has thrown touchdown passes on 8 percent of his attempts, the best in the NFL this season and by far the best mark of his career. And after getting sacked a career-high 41 times last year, Lawrence has gotten much more comfortable reading the pass rush in his second year in Coen's offense and has only been sacked 13 times this season.

Lawrence's numbers would look even better if the Jaguars weren't so often taking their foot off the gas late in games because they're blowing opponents out. Lawrence has 1,196 yards and 12 touchdowns in the first halves of games this season, but he only has 736 yards and six touchdowns in the second halves of games.

The Jaguars currently have the fourth-best odds to win the Super Bowl, and Lawrence has the fifth-best odds to win MVP. That might be underselling them, and him. The Jaguars may just be the best team, with the best quarterback, in the NFL right now.

#2824. Justin Jefferson says his frustration came from "wanting to win"

Vikings receiver Justin Jefferson engaged in a rare display of frustration late in Sunday’s 19-15 loss to the Lions. He also didn’t talk to reporters after the game, possibly to avoid saying things that would underscore what he was feeling in the moment.

Four days later, Jefferson spoke to the media — and the No. 1 topic was his apparent mood during Minnesota’s first loss of the season.

“It was wanting to win,” Jefferson said, via Kevin Seifert of ESPN, “and I felt like we had plenty of opportunities to win that game and we only hurt ourselves in multiple ways. It’s just wanting better from the whole entire offense especially. And I feel like the potential and the guys that we have in that room is something very, very special. I feel like we’re wasting that if not going out there executing the plays that we have called and just not living to that standard that we feel like we live up to every single day.”

Jefferson, who always says all the right things about his quarterbacks, said all the right things about Kyler Murray, whose performance against Detroit largely contributed to the failure to score more than 15 points.

“I feel like Kyler has continued to grow,” Jefferson said. “I feel like Kyler is continuing to get comfortable with this offense. And I feel like the plays that are there are plays that he’s well capable of making. And those are plays that we’ve seen him make multiple times throughout the season, throughout practice and in training camp as well. So we definitely have faith in him. We have confidence in him to go out there and be that guy that we need him and want him to be.

“But all in all, it’s just executing our plays and just coming ready to play. And I feel like once he’s back out there and he gets more comfortable with the system, more comfortable with just throwing to these different type of receivers, then I feel like he’s going to look a lot better in [reporters’] eyes. But we see that every single day. We see that type of Kyler that we need out there on Sundays every single day. So just bringing that on Sundays. We’re behind him. We’re confident in him, so we just going to keep riding with him.”

For now, the Vikings will ride with Carson Wentz, while Murray is out with a hamstring injury. And Wentz has proven that, of all the quarterbacks who have played for the Vikings since Sam Darnold left for Seattle after the 2024 season, Wentz knows how to get the ball to Jefferson.

Soft bench or not, Wentz has an opportunity to stay on the field if he makes the plays that Murray didn’t on Sunday. Plays that, by the time the game was on the line, coach Kevin O’Connell didn’t allow Murray to try to make.

The one moment that resonates from Sunday’s game wasn’t anything Murray did or failed to do. It came from O’Connell’s decision to punt from the Minnesota 33-yard line on fourth and five with 3:01 to play. Given the manner in which the Lions were running the ball, the likelihood of getting another opportunity to score a touchdown was slim.

Put simply, if O’Connell didn’t trust Murray to gain five yards with the game on the line, O’Connell shouldn’t entrust the starting job to Murray.

For now, Murray technically can’t play due to injury. It’s hard not to wonder whether, if Murray had made the plays needed to outscore the Lions on Sunday, he’d be playing on Monday night despite the injured hamstring.

#2823. Observations after Sixers beat Bulls to reach East-leading 7-1

Observations after Sixers beat Bulls to reach East-leading 7-1 originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers kept up their hot start to the season Monday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena, reaching 7-1 with a 126-107 win against the Bulls.

All five of the Sixers' starters scored in double figures. Tyrese Maxey posted 26 points on 10-for-15 shooting and 11 assists. Jaylen Brown tallied a season-best 25 points and 11 rebounds.

VJ Edgecombe's 21 points were a new season high. LeBron James recorded 15 points, nine assists and seven boards.

Bulls rookie Caleb Wilson had 24 points and seven rebounds.

Joel Embiid (15 points, eight rebounds) had been listed as questionable with an official designation of "right foot plantar fascia injury management." He sat out Saturday on the second night of a back-to-back for the Sixers' win over the Hornets.

"Plantar is a little bit of a come and go type of thing," Sixers head coach Nick Nurse told reporters pregame. "They're just trying to manage it. It's very painful, if you've ever had it. It can kind of come and go out of nowhere. So we're just trying to manage the pain with that, be as smart as we can."

Nurse told reporters that Dominick Barlow is set to see a specialist Tuesday about the back injury that's sidelined him to start the season.

"He's been on court a little bit … not a ton of moving around," Nurse said. "I think they want to get to tomorrow's appointment. Hopefully, it'll be positive and we can get into his workouts a little bit."

The Sixers will begin a three-game road trip Wednesday when they visit the Pistons. Here are observations on their victory Monday:

After Embiid blitzed a Bulls pick-and-roll, Maxey picked off Matas Buzelis' hurried pass to get the Sixers rolling in transition and James jammed home the team's first field goal.

Edgecombe got a slam soon after James grabbed a defensive rebound and the Sixers again pushed the pace. The Sixers scored six quick fast-break points, leading the Bulls to burn an early timeout, and James' long-distance feeds were a major asset.

"If you're open, he's going to pass it," Edgecombe said of James. "The main thing is just being ready. Tonight I had to run and go get 'em. If you're open and he sees you, he's going to pass the ball."

Edgecombe had a dunk-heavy first quarter. He threw down his second when Dean Wade nabbed a steal and dropped off a typically selfless dish to the Sixers' explosive second-year guard, whose slam put the team up 22-13.

The Sixers have an abundance of dangerous options in the open floor, Edgecombe included. As he's already shown with his continued clutch shotmaking, the 21-year-old won't become anything resembling a non-factor offensively this year as a byproduct of the Sixers' enhanced star power.

Over the team's first seven games, Edgecombe had averaged 11.3 points. He scored 11 in the first period on 5-for-5 shooting.

Adem Bona missed a dunk early in the second quarter, which stung a bit more when Jalen Smith drilled a three-pointer seconds later.

Bona remained the Sixers' main backup center. He had a poor first-half stint overall amid a largely negative start to his third season. The 23-year-old big man played well in the Sixers' victory over the Bucks, posting six points, 13 rebounds and three blocks. Outside of that, his season has been sparse on bright moments so far. It's reasonable to wonder when Nurse might turn to alternatives like Jabari Walker, who played a good game Saturday in Charlotte, or try James again at the five.

The Bulls outscored the Sixers by eight points in Bona's first run, cutting their derficit to 40-38. Chicago went in front with a three by former Sixer Buddy Hield.

The Sixers regained the advantage late in the second quarter. Maxey and James each were excellent as passers in the first half, combining for 14 assists and three turnovers. James fired the ball to Wade for a corner three that gave the Sixers a 60-52 lead.

Following a third-quarter Embiid fadeaway jumper and two James lay-ins, the Sixers were up 17 points.

The Bulls cut the Sixers' lead down to 11 points by the start of the fourth quarter. With Bona still struggling and on four fouls, Wade began the fourth at center. Bona then briefly spelled Wade before being whistled for his fifth foul and taking a seat. Embiid ultimately wasn't needed for any of the fourth period and only logged 25 minutes.

Embiid said postgame that he was not available to return to the action in the fourth and has been feeling his plantar fasciitis on the court. The seven-time All-Star's health is clearly not close to 100 percent.

"I was on a minutes restriction," he said. "(The foot) has been going like that for the past few weeks. It's painful. Just got to manage it.

"If it flares up pretty bad, got to take a step back. We've been able to manage it, but it has its ups and downs."

The Sixers' lead got as low as eight points, but Chicago did not shoot well enough from three-point range (26.3 percent) or have sufficient firepower to sustain a meaningful comeback run. The bottom line is the Sixers are in a different class than the Bulls, who fell to 1-6.

As for the Sixers, they'll wake up Tuesday morning at the top of the Eastern Conference standings.

"You've got some of these nights where you kind of call them professional wins. …You look at the records and all that kind of stuff, but they have a lot of talent," Nurse said. "A lot of these teams play a way that's a little scary. It's fast and it's furious, lots of threes. … They're going to keep coming at you, high-possession games. #2820. Jaguars' point differential of +108 this season is 50 points better than any other team

No NFL team is dominating opponents like the Jacksonville Jaguars.

After blowing out the Ravens 33-10 on Thursday night, the Jaguars have now outscored their opponents by a cumulative score of 229-121 this season. That’s a point differential of +108, by far the best in the NFL.

The team with the second-best point differential in the NFL is the 49ers, at +58. The Jaguars’ point differential is 50 points better than the next-best team.

At 6-2, the Jaguars do not have the best record in the league, as the Bills, 49ers and Vikings are all 6-1. The 49ers are favored to beat the Raiders and improve to 7-1, and the Bills and Vikings play each other on Monday night, so the winner will be 7-1.

But at the midway point of the season, point differential is a better indication of a team’s quality, and a better predictor of a team’s future success, than win-loss record. That’s because with as small a sample size as half a season, a few plays in a few close games can skew the won-loss record, but a few plays don’t skew point differential. Historically, the teams that prove to be the best over the course of a season are the teams that win some blowouts, even if they also lose some close games.

Winning blowouts and losing close games is exactly what the Jaguars do. Both of the Jaguars’ losses were one-possession games that were tied in the fourth quarter, while the Jaguars’ wins have included some massive blowouts: The Jaguars’ 35-point win over the Colts was the biggest blowout of this NFL season, their 29-point win over the Patriots was the fourth-biggest blowout in the NFL this season, their 24-point win over the Browns was the seventh-biggest blowout in the NFL this season, and Thursday night’s 23-point win over the Ravens was the 11th-biggest blowout in the NFL this season.

The Jaguars have won four games by more than 21 points this season; no other team has more than one win by more than 21 points.

Jacksonville has a 3.5-game lead in the AFC South, and six of the Jaguars’ nine remaining games are against opponents with a losing record. They’re poised to run away with their division, perhaps earn the No. 1 seed in the AFC, and maybe blow some teams out in the playoffs just like they have in the regular season.

#2816. ‘I'm finding my footing': Jaylen Brown's role taking shape with Sixers

'I'm finding my footing': Jaylen Brown's role taking shape with Sixers originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Jaylen Brown has spent the opening weeks of the season describing the Sixers as a work in progress.

He offered a similarly humble perspective Monday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena. His performance, however, provided the clearest look yet at how he can influence this group while sharing the floor with the club's other established stars.

Brown finished with 25 points, 11 rebounds and five assists in the Sixers' 126-107 win over the Chicago Bulls. He shot 9 for 15 from the field, made four three-pointers and did not commit a turnover.

Five of his rebounds came on the offensive end, an area Brown has emphasized while the Sixers continue piecing together their frontcourt rotation.

"Just a mindset," Brown said. "Just trying to create extra opportunities for my team. As we're trying to patch together our fives and our front line, I try to make an extra contribution and emphasis on the glass."

Brown has also been careful about how he describes his place on a roster that already belonged to Joel Embiid and Tyrese Maxey.

Maxey scored 15 of his 26 points in the fourth quarter Monday, continuing his torrid start to the season. He has led the Sixers in scoring while being the only starter to appear in all eight games.

Brown is not interested in interrupting that.

"Maxey's been leading the way, 100 percent," Brown said. "He's been here. This is his team. Him and Joel have been here for a while, so the mindset has been to complement those guys. I'm finding my footing, but Maxey has been leading the way for sure."

Brown's footing looked firm against Chicago.

Beyond his scoring, he helped the Sixers control the glass, moved the ball within an offense that generated 23 assists during the first half and supplied the physicality Nick Nurse expects from him.

"The dude is tough and he wins," Nurse said. "I'll take that all day long. The degree of difficulty on some of the shots he hit was really amazing. I thought he pounded the glass and got some key rebounds. Makes a lot of winning plays. Man, he's a winner."

Brown spent the first 10 years of his career in Boston. He won a championship there, reached another NBA Finals and grew from a 20-year-old prospect into one of the league's premier two-way wings.

Moving into a new system alongside James, Embiid and Maxey was never going to be seamless.

"I mean, he's fitting in along with all of us," James said. "We're getting better and better. It's not going to happen overnight. He spent his first 10 years in a system in Boston, in the city, so it's going to take some adjustment.

"It takes adjustment for him. It's going to take adjustment for the rest of the guys that joined this franchise as well. But tonight was a great step."

James pointed to Brown's "pressure, his shot-making ability, his rebounding ability" and his professionalism.

Brown's early influence has extended beyond his production.

The Sixers entered Monday with one of the NBA's best half-court defenses. Brown has been one of the group's most persistent voices, stressing communication, preparation and attention to opposing players' tendencies.

"That's the part that I care about the most as a group, not individually," Brown said. "Having a mentality night in and night out, respecting your opponent, respecting the game, making sure that we are executing our coverages, we're being clear in our communication and then we're also taking away tendencies on a night-to-night basis.

"Those things I just explained are over 50 percent of the battle."

Brown understands that maintaining those details across an 82-game schedule will require more than reminders.

"A little bit of accountability," he said. "You learn different guys require different things. How you communicate with each guy may be a little different, but accountability for sure and confrontation if need be.

"The offense is going to be what it's going to be, but our defense has got to be non-negotiable. That's something I say all the time. Non-negotiable. You want to be a good team, defense is non-negotiable."

The Sixers showed both sides of their defensive potential Monday.

They built a double-digit lead during the first half, allowed Chicago to score 36 points in the second quarter and then created separation after halftime. Philadelphia held the Bulls to 20 points in the third quarter before pulling away in the fourth.

Brown did not celebrate their ability to raise their intensity after it slipped.

"I don't like that we have that," he said. "It's good that we have shown the potential, but we've got to keep that switch on. It doesn't work like that where you just flip the switch.

"It can catch up to us and it can bite us against a better team or on a night that we're not being as crisp on offense. It can't be a switch just because we're playing a lesser opponent or whatever the case may be. We've got to make sure that mentality is from the beginning to end. Can't skip any steps."

That urgency accompanies considerable optimism.

Brown said the Sixers enjoy playing together. He loves when James grabs a rebound because "he's like a quarterback," capable of launching an outlet pass or immediately pushing the pace.

The group is learning when to attack, when to move the ball and how to avoid hesitating in its effort to play unselfishly.

"It's a lot of talent, man," Brown said. "We like each other, and we're just kind of building that chemistry of how we can get this thing to a well-oiled machine. I think we're taking steps forward every single day."

The Sixers are 7-1 despite Brown believing those steps remain incomplete. They have won close games, erased sizable deficits and received important contributions from different players.

Brown's performance Monday showed another version of how their pieces can fit.

"We still have a long way to go to being a really, really solid, great team," Brown said. "But we've been able to win some games. We started out the season great, 7-1, and you haven't seen our best version yet.

#2813. Giants-Eagles matchup: How does QB Joe Milton change the equation?

The 4-2-1 New York Giants travel to Philadelphia this weekend to face the 2–6 Philadelphia Eagles, who enter the matchup on a six-game losing streak. Philadelphia is coming off a disappointing 27–10 loss to the Washington Commanders on Sunday Night Football in Week 8.

Things are unraveling in Philadelphia. The Eagles are dealing with a rash of injuries and have switched from quarterback Tanner McKee to Joe Milton. Head coach Nick Sirianni is facing mounting questions from the media about offensive coordinator Sean Mannion, while general manager Howie Roseman has traded valuable assets in exchange for draft capital. To put it simply, things are far from sunny in Philadelphia.

Still, the Eagles will look to defend their home turf against a Giants franchise that hasn't won at Lincoln Financial Field since 2013. New York enters the matchup well-rested after its bye week, presenting an opportunity to snap that frustrating losing streak. And with the John Harbaugh era bringing a different identity and renewed expectations to the Giants, this team may finally have what it takes to change the narrative.

The Eagles' offense has struggled all season. Philadelphia ranks 30th in the league in points per game, with an average of just 17.1 points. They're 29th in total yards (2,122 yards), 32nd in yards per game (265 yards), and they're last in yards per play (4.4 YPP).

Philadelphia ranks 24th in passing yards per game (196.4) and 27th in rushing yards per game (88.1). They have a 37.3% third-down conversion rate, which ranks 26th in the league.

Tanner McKee has completed 63.2% of his passes for 638 yards with a pair of touchdowns and interceptions. Joe Milton, though, poses a much different skill set that the Giants must account for. DeVonta Smith has missed a handful of games, including the loss to Washington last week; he still leads the team with 310 receiving yards.

Saquon Barkley is hobbled and played on a pitch count last week. He leads the Eagles with 274 rushing yards (4.9 YPC), with two rushing touchdowns. Elijah Mitchell is the backup running back with Tank Bigsby, Will Shipley, and Dameon Pierce all on injured reserve.

Milton played three seasons at Michigan dating back to 2018 before he transferred to Tennessee. He threw for 2,813 yards with 20 touchdowns and five interceptions and a 64.7% completion rate in Josh Heupel's offense back in 2023; he also rushed for 299 yards and seven touchdowns that year. Milton spent time with the Patriots, Cowboys, and now the Eagles.

Saquon Barkley played 32% of the snaps in Week 8. He touched the football often in his limited snaps over the last two weeks – he played 15% of snaps in Week 7. Mitchell is the primary backup now, and Jaydon Blue played 12% of snaps last week. The running situation – including the push up front from the line – has been poor.

Smith missed the last two weeks, and the two weeks prior to Week 6. Dontayvion Wicks hasn't played since Week 6. It's been the rookies, Makai Lemon and Darius Cooper, who have played more than 90% of the snaps over the last two weeks. Both players have flashed.

Hollywood Brown and Elijah Moore were the only other two wide receivers to play snaps against Washington, who operated heavier personnel packages without Smith. Tight end Dallas Goedert played 80% of the snaps, as Johnny Mundt and Eli Stowers both played 19% of snaps. Grant Calcaterra played 17% of snaps.

Jordan Mailata is the starting left tackle with rookie Markel Bell starting on the right side; Lane Johnson retired a few weeks ago, forcing Bell into the starting lineup. Tyler Steen mans the right guard spot, with Landon Dickerson playing left guard; Dickerson has been playing through a pectoral injury. Drew Kendall is the starting center now that Cam Jurgens is no longer an Eagle after he was traded to the Baltimore Ravens.

Starting Milton could provide the Eagles with a spark. The 6-foot-5, 245-pound quarterback is an excellent athlete with a howitzer arm, but he's bounced around practice squads and hasn't found consistency yet. Still, his mobility and strength in the pocket could allow him to escape the Giants' rush. It's an exciting move for Philadelphia — all things considered — but he's never proven consistent with timing, accuracy, and other nuances of the quarterback position, albeit he's just 26 years old.

New York has blitzed at a 36.6% rate this season, which ranks second only behind the Minnesota Vikings. I expect the Giants to dial up the pressure against the young quarterback, with a heavy middle-of-the-field closed approach. The Eagles have struggled offensively, but the Giants must focus on stopping Barkley when he is on the field.

The Giants can run man-to-man situational defense and focus on Cover-3, with a focus on stopping the run. Adjustments to middle-of-the-field-open defenses will happen in third-and-long situations. Fire-zone blitzes and a pre-snap loaded line of scrimmage should be employed in an attempt to force mistakes from the young quarterback.

New York's cornerbacks should press up on the line if Philadelphia attempts to run quick game often, as plenty of teams have attempted to run against the Giants. If pressure starts to get home on Milton and New York establishes a lead, the Giants can sit comfortably in zone to force check-downs underneath, as Washington did at the end of their win against Philadelphia.

If Philadelphia leans on more 12 personnel, especially with Eli Stowers, how do the Giants respond? Base or Nickel? Since New York will likely want to stop the run, they may respond with a heavier base package – five-man front. Philadelphia may look to try and get Stowers isolated against a linebacker or safety in those heavier tight end packages.

The Eagles' offensive line has been susceptible in both pass protection and as run blockers, relative to what we're accustomed to seeing every year. The Giants have to maintain the level of knock-back and physicality that they had against Houston. If they can do that, the Giants shouldn't have a problem winning the game.

The Giants are the better football team. Still, winning in Philadelphia hasn't been an easy venture for the Giants. I believe they get over the hump and win convincingly in Philadelphia. Pick: 30-13, Giants.
